In the year 2026, in a world increasingly filled with fucking generative A.I. bullshit, Cats is more important than ever. It is a uniquely human piece. It is the product of decades of weird, blank check-level artists iterating on and interpreting each other's bizarre art in ways that frankly make no fucking sense. It is a film built on incredible artistic hubris. It is full of baffling choices. It is absurd that it exists at all, especially that it took so many years and so many versions of Cats for it to finally be so soundly rejected by people. I love it. I love sharing it with people, watching their reactions, explaining to them why this movie has my heart and reflects my soul. I love it. What you say of Cats , you say of me, of my family, my loved ones. I am not a believer in the existence of the butthole cut. But the mere idea that it could exist, that people might believe that it's something that Tom Hooper would've done if given the chance—the older I get, the more beautiful I think that is. There are still original artistic ideas, even amidst "safe" Hollywood choices, adaptations of adaptations, art can be made that is so unlike anything a human mind has conceived that it makes people believe in the butthole cut. Cats is so mind-blowing that it makes the inconceivable become conceivable. Thank you, Cats . Thank you to everyone in my life who is willing to watch it with me. We know each other better because of it. Thank you for caring enough to look directly into my heart.

Rebel Wilson and James Corden do improvisational comedy with all the ardor and skill of drama club kids whose families have just been taken hostage at gunpoint. Yet, everything else in this film has the feeling of watching a two hour cutaway gag from prime seasons of The Simpsons; it takes very little imagination to picture Troy McClure starring in this. When I saw this in theaters for the first time, I kept leaning over to my best friend and whispering, with unbridled exhilaration, "They made this into a movie!" Tom Hooper is not a talented director, which makes him perfect for this movie as a workmanlike, or even well made, version of this material would be forgetable to all but a handful of the most debased musical theater perverts. In Hooper's other pictures, he has a baseline level of competence more-or-less sufficient to overcome his penchant for deeply strange choices. Choices like like throwing dutch angles into his period prestige films-- or having the section of the John Adams miniseries where the title characeter goes to France mostly revolve around an elderly woman in clown make up jack off Benjamin Franklin in a tub (to be fair she could've also been milking his prostate; we don't get to see what's going on under the water). Here, however, the adulation Hooper received from his previous movies fried his brain; his hubris is archetypal. Every creative choice he makes big or small, is not merely off-- or sub-optimal-- they are objectively wrong. And that’s what makes Cats so special. There are many bad films, but they usually do some things right-- or alternatively they display a childlike lack of technical ability that reads as charming. Cats, inextricably, lands in neither category. It’s shaped like a movie. It has the bones, sinew, structure, and grammar of a movie in the way something like Birdemic or The Room never would. But despite its (mostly) quite talented cast, it's a series of wildly incorrect miscalculations that immediately begin to compound on one another and do not stop until the credits roll. I have never seen another movie like it and I watch it every chance I get. #Skimblegang

images that are produced make you feel like you're in a surreal state, almost similar to that of the work from David Lynch, and sometimes even surpassing that level of surrealism. a great example Dench, James Corden and many others of the cast present their immense talent at horrendous singing that sounds like a rat getting squished by a foot every 5 seconds (apparently Judi Dench can actually sing but no evidence of that could be found in this). it sounds unpleasant, yes, but it ultimately does a great job at making the audience squirm and curl up in fear in their seat (it happened to me). the cinematography is also one of the best in the cinema history, with (insert DP name here) being able to capture the film's surreal aesthetic. so is the production design, which takes audience immersion to a whole new level. sets are designed to make the audience feel as if they are at the same height of the cats, adding to the incredibly surreal experience of the film. to end my review, i would like to mention that Cats could be viewed as a terrible film, even the worst of the decade. there are plenty of reasons to think that, and it is totally up to you. but when you look at a film's intention, and at the final product, and realise that the film accomplished exactly what it set out do, in this case to cause discomfort, you know for a fact that it is truly a masterpiece. please give this underrated gem the money it lost at the box office by purchasing it on Blu-ray.

Tratto dal ponderoso romanzo di Paulo Lins (600 pagine), il film risulta fallimentare sotto tutti i punti di vista. Perché se è vero che le favelas di Rio de Janeiro rappresentano il luogo di un degrado sociale e morale certo profondo e di non facile soluzione, è altrettanto vero che non è con questa operazione che si può sperare di portare un minimo aiuto alla causa. Non risparmiando niente sul piano visivo per quanto attiene a brutalità e violenze e anzi lasciandole uniche, incontrastate protagoniste, il regista vorrebbe far passare l'idea che lui si limita a riprendere la realtà senza intervenire: ma l'eccesso di realismo scavalca il confine della credibilità e fa diventare il racconto più finto della finzione. Dominano allora personaggi come macchiette in mezzo ad un quadro di vita che non restituisce mai la complessità della situazione, essendo insisitito in una sola direzione, quella del crimine e della perdita della vita da adolescenti. Parziale e nichilista, il film accumula solo sconcezze e volgarità, compiacendosi di mostrare bambini sempre più piccoli in giro per le strade pronti ad uccidere, e così impedendo di mettere in piedi qualunque riflessione su quelle situazioni gravi che si vorrebbero (forse, ma non è sicuro) denunciare. Dal punto di vista pastorale, il film è da valutare come inaccettabile, e fortemente negativo.

Can we actually find value in a film that while yes shows the violence people go through when their material needs aren’t met, but doesn’t actually fully call out the cause of the violence? I don’t think so. Especially when the violence towards the men, women, and children is shown as just a symptom and not actually done tactfully. To not have any discussion about the cause of the violence is because of state and police violence, because of class systems, racism, and sexism is irresponsible. Vague pointing at police is not enough. This film says violence begets violence and that right there is the most violent part of this film. These people deserve more. And if all we do is witness the violence can we say we are any better? I don’t think so.

I can’t imagine many of the people who live in The City Of God at the time actually saw this theatrically. And I imagine they would find this distasteful. This is all quite gauche and feels exploitative of real poverty and the trap of poverty. The film deals with race quite strangely as well in a way that made me feel a little bit uncomfortable. Im not really a fan of the style of this either, it’s all very flashy but it kind of makes the characters never feel fully realised. They don’t feel like real people because the movie is more interested in being stylised poverty porn exploitation than a story about people. The idea of gazing at disproportionally black poverty and violence and killing is not interesting to me. Especially when it isnt made for or by the community it is depicting the suffering of. The way death and dead bodies are handled in this film intentionally lacks a level of weight i think to alienate people and upset them. But an image  containing only viscera  divorces the humanity of death and turns it into a spectacle to gaze at. If this came out in an English speaking environment i think people would be more critical of this. Most English speaking audiences don’t really watch films in other languages. I think there is an element of this being an incredibly easy to understand narrative and stylistically familiar enough that more people would give this a shot as a “foreign film”. Which i think lends to a level of exoticism to how some people interact with and engage with the film. Of the few negative reviews i have bothered glancing at a lot of them seem to come from Brazil. There are other crime films i share this criticism with. However there are still several crime films that feel connected enough to the communities depicted in them, to where I feel they are less problematic. The gaze and regard in which this film is held in to me reads as somewhat colonial. The Auteurs and audience domination and extraction of respect, life and humanity in exchange for a narrative that allows people to have their “Harrowing” movie where they get to watch vicariously through an audience surrogate. Where is the framework of media analysis with the response to this film? I genuinely think audiences collectively should scrutinise this film so much more. During my film course at uni there have been several films we have seen where we interrogate how we felt about the film we just watched, we process what it was saying, what it meant, and even at times analysed where the point of view of its conception came from. And sometimes this encompassed the ethics of a film’s conception. And oftentimes this inherently led to the concepts of class dynamics and racism. This is a film that is quite frankly begging for this level of interrogation. And the overwhelming majority of people simply don’t care enough to analyse how the film made them feel the way it did or what it has to say about the context in which the film was made in.

I was afraid this would be the case. Right from the start, we are introduced to the main characters, Goodfellas-style, Americanized and flashy. Fernando Meirelles stopped caring about being vocal about crime and poverty once he got the check, and I wouldn't have guessed otherwise. I find this film similar to La Haine in political and contextual terms, but one death in La Haine made me think for days, whereas there is a death every minute in City of God. It's not nearly as moving because the characters have no depth. Every person and the city are reduced to their worst, and it was painful to sit through this viewing. And of course, it doesn't pass the Bechdel test, why would it? It's disappointing that City of God is still so acclaimed. I guess the illusion of fatalism masquerading as social critique is too strong to break.

“I honestly don't understand the overwhelming praise for City of God. While the film has impressive camera work and a fast-paced style, I found it exhausting rather than engaging. The constant violence, brutal characters, and endless cycle of crime make it feel more like a long sequence of shocking moments than a meaningful story. The characters are difficult to connect with because so many of them are defined by cruelty and survival, leaving little emotional depth for the audience to hold on to. The movie seems more interested in showing chaos and brutality than exploring the people behind it. The storytelling style, with its rapid editing and nonstop narration, can also feel distracting and overcomplicated. Instead of creating a powerful emotional experience, it sometimes feels like the film is trying too hard to prove how gritty and intense it can be. Although it has technical strengths, City of God was not an enjoyable watch for me. It is violent, overwhelming, and far too focused on misery to be the masterpiece many people claim it is.”

Очередной недопонятый мною шедевр. Как будто самая обычная криминальная драма из 70х-80х, но действия не в США, а в Бразилии. Ну не работает больше такой жанр, тем более в Бразилии. В стандартной криминальной драме должен быть слом главного героя, он показывает, что криминал и криминальная среда просто уничтожает его морально и потом физически. В этом фильме есть такие персонажи с похожей судьбой, но они оказываются антагонистами. А главный герой поучаствовал во всех криминальных зарубах, но остался в выигрыше и теперь снимает на камеру как бандюганы негры друг друга истребляют. Криминал есть, драмы практически нет. I've wanted to watch this for years and years, and yet I never did. Maybe there was a reason for that. City of God brims with flair and technique, and there is nary a moment when the image and sound presented aren't well rendered and constructed. But therein lies the issue with this film. It feels too constructed, too amalgamated. The result of a heap of story material set ablaze specifically to hide from sincerity. Is the story true? To a turn, as many of these kinds of stories are. I think where this one falters is that it never seems to stop to consider that it's got one foot in the door of stylized imaginings of a roughly relatable cinematic narrative, and the other in the door of gritty depiction of the lives of the sub-altern. It tends to choose style more than anything else, and in doing so leaves a lot on the table. The flair and flash of its photography, cutting and acting lose quite a bit of their impact by the time you see the 15th or so callous murder--a weightlessness that it feels like the film encourages after a fashion. Simply put: there isn't enough story behind the pomp and circumstance to keep the style engaging. The narrative feels less like a cohesive tableau and more like a series of loosely connected vignettes that are united by violence and excess and not by character presence or investment. Glad I watched it, but I can't say I'm happy with what I watched.

City of God is executed with such technical skill that it almost feels like exhibitionism on the filmmakers’ part. We get split-screens, we get sharply edited montages, we get scenes shown twice from different perspectives, and we get some long, magnificent tracking shots, often through crowds, that must have been almost impossible to pull off. It’s really slick. But what is it? Is it a brutal gangster flick, or a social drama about degradation that carries genuine anthropological weight? The easy answer would be to say it’s both, and the vast swathes of critics and fans who think the movie’s terrific would be sure to express such a sentiment. I’m not so sure. Especially in its second hour, I felt the movie leaned more heavily toward the first description than the second, as its plot became denser and its level of sensationalist violence intensified. Thematically, and often in execution, too, it’s very similar to the TV show The Wire, and I can’t be the first to point that out, though contemporary critics would not have had the luxury of such a comparison. Inevitably, it is not able to say as much in two hours as The Wire was able to say over five seasons and fifty episodes. But, for one thing, The Wire breathed human life into its antagonists, and showed us that their actions are not always motivated by greed or viciousness. This cannot be said for City of God’s principal villain Lil Ze, who laughingly dispatches crying children on-camera and for whom passing jealousy is a perfectly good motive to rape a stranger while making her boyfriend watch. Sympathetic characters- Benny, for example, or Rocket, are conveniently never shown engaging in violent acts at all; we are left in no doubt which characters we are supposed to like and which characters we aren’t. Subsequently, it lacks The Wire’s more complex, incisive dynamics. On a cinema screen in 2002, when here in the UK I was still technically not old enough to watch it, it might have been pretty wild. Oldboy too. But though I did prefer it to Oldboy, ultimately I felt that, with its swathes of characters, its whip-smart edits, its proliferating abundance of death and carnage, the film was using sensory overload in an attempt to steamroller me into exhilaration. As it is, on a small screen 20 years later, I don’t feel the film had the kind of power that it appeared to be striving for. It’s not a bad film- far from it. It’s actually a very good one if the material happens to resonate with you. But what does it have to tell us, really, other than that the slums of Rio are terrible beyond belief, where the police have no power, and where the most amoral of a given generation tend to be the ones that rise up through the ranks and end up essentially running the place? I don’t know, really. That does seem to be the main heft of the piece. And there’s a titillating aspect to City of God that sits uncomfortably with its apparent status as a social document, a ‘message from the front line’. There is a relentless, sun-drenched velocity to City of God that tricks you into thinking you’re watching a kinetic crime epic, right up until you realize every scene is quietly mourning. What hits hardest on a rewatch isn't just the breathless editing or the electric, samba infused soundtrack it’s how the film treats youth. Kids in the favela aren't given a grace period to just figure things out; they’re forced into adult archetypes before their voices even break. Rocket’s camera lens becomes his only real shield, a way to witness the chaos without letting it consume him entirely, while Lil Zé treats fear as the only currency that matters You could argue it occasionally risks hyper stylizing real world trauma at times, the late 90s post MTV sheen almost feels too sleek for the gravel and sweat it’s documenting. But underneath all that frantic, kinetic energy is a deeply human pulse. It barely lets you catch your breath, not just to thrill you, but because the kids on screen never got to catch theirs either

City of God is a Brazilian crime drama directed by Fernando Meirelles and Kátia Lund. It is based on real events and portrays life in the Cidade de Deus (City of God) favela in Rio de Janeiro from the 1960s to the early 1980s. The story follows Buscapé (Rocket), a shy and intelligent boy who dreams of becoming a photographer instead of joining the world of crime around him. Through his eyes, the audience witnesses how poverty, violence, and gang rivalries shape the lives of children and teenagers in the favela. At the same time, another boy, Li'l Zé (Zé Pequeno), grows up to become one of the most feared and ruthless gang leaders in the neighbourhood. His desire for power and control leads to brutal conflicts with rival gangs, creating a cycle of violence that affects everyone around him. As Rocket tries to avoid crime and pursue a better future, he documents the reality of life in the favela through his camera. His photographs eventually become a way for the outside world to see the harsh conditions and violence of City of God. City of God is widely regarded as one of the greatest crime films ever made. Its fast-paced storytelling, realistic performances, and striking cinematography create an intense and emotionally powerful experience. The performances feel authentic, with many actors coming from communities similar to those depicted. The nonlinear storytelling keeps the narrative engaging. The cinematography and editing are energetic and memorable. The film realistically portrays how poverty and limited opportunities can trap young people in cycles of violence without glorifying crime. The movie contains strong violence, disturbing scenes, and mature themes, making it suitable only for mature audiences. Some viewers may find its rapid editing and multiple characters challenging to follow at first.

Really cool movie. I really liked it and it gave me a unique kind of feeling I don’t really get with most other movies. It’s rough, down right appalling and hard to watch at some points but for all the right reasons. I liked the fact that, while displaying some genuinely shocking things that most people would’ve never experienced or been exposed to, it didn’t glamorise them, focus too much on them or use them simply as shock value. It treated them as completely typical time and time again which I think is how most people growing up in that area (and the inspiration for the movie) saw these things. After a while, you started seeing things the same way. The cinematography was also really cool and effective. Particularly liked the club scene. Why not 5 stars? I mean I just didn’t ‘wow’ me as much as some of the 5 star movies I have. This movie reminded me a bit of The Infierno, where the cycle of violence never truly ends—it just gets passed on to the next generation. In City of God, though, the city was literally lawless, so the violence didn't have to wait for one generation to die before continuing. The ambition and brutality were simply passed from one group of kids in the favela to the next. Li'l Zé is one of the most despicable, disgusting, and pathetic characters I've ever seen in a movie. The fact that the film reveals at the end that it's based on a true story hit me hard. People like that are out there. Even though he's a victim of the environment he grew up in, I don't feel any sympathy for him—not even when he was a child. He seemed to have the personality of a psychopath from the very beginning. It's incredible that Bené genuinely enjoyed the company of someone as pathetic as Zé. Not even his death made me feel any better because that rain of bullets wasn't nearly enough punishment for all the pain and terror he caused. Talking about the movie itself, I understand why it's considered a masterpiece. It certainly was for me too. I'm not new to this kind of non-chronological storytelling, but saving the opening scene until the last 15 minutes of the movie felt incredible. I thought it was going to be a Casino situation, where the opening scene doesn't come back until about an hour and a half into the film.

Incredible movie. Emotional, funny, intense, brilliant. Cinematography was marvelous, dialogue was clever and powerful, story was well-narrated and well-presented, and the characters felt like real people living real lives. I was totally engrossed in the movie the whole time. I was initially shocked to find out it was based on a true story because of how cinematically perfect the plot was, but then it immediately made sense to me why everything in the movie felt so real. Terrific watch, contains every element of a perfect story.

Proof that the cameraman really never dies… LMAO On a real note, this is an absolute masterpiece. From the cinematography to the acting to the pacing, it is as close to perfection as a film can get. I spent a good 45 minutes after finishing it trying to come up with a single complaint, and not one thing came to mind. From the opening sequence with its incredible 360° transition and beautifully composed still shots to the emotionally devastating ending framed from behind, City of God is one of the best movies I’ve ever seen and, dare I say, the most creatively executed. There are so many things to love about this movie, but after doing my due diligence and learning that roughly 70% of the cast consisted of local children with little or no acting experience, I appreciated it even more. It makes the performances feel that much more authentic. It’s hard to write a review when there are so many aspects deserving of praise, but one thing I have to highlight is how interconnected the story is. There are at least 25 meaningful characters, yet somehow every single one leaves an impression. It doesn’t matter how much screen time they have—their presence is remembered and their role in the story feels important. I’d compare it to The Godfather , another film with an enormous cast, but I actually think City of God handles its ensemble even better. Every storyline feels purposeful, and none of the characters get lost in the chaos. I could easily write four more paragraphs about this film, but to keep it short, if you asked me to describe it in one sentence, I’d simply say it’s as close to a perfect film as I’ve ever seen. “Wanna get shot in the hand or the foot?” 9.9/10

What an amazing watch. This movie perfectly enthralls and immerses you into the setting and time period of 1970s Rio slums. This movie is ambitious as fuck; so many characters and different plot lines being passed back and forth. Lots of moving parts here. It executes it all PERFECTLY. The ensemble cast is flawless with each character leaving an impact and the vibes are HIGH the entire time. Brutal gang violence never seemed so fun! The story sucks you in with characters you love and root for and characters you want to get turned into swiss cheese, stuff that makes you laugh and stuff that makes you wanna look away, but it’s also just lowkey a vibe. It feels like this could be a great movie to hangout to, and because so much is going on at once it could be amazing on a rewatch. This movie literally has it all I can’t recommend it enough. I kept saying it felt like the Brazilian Goodfellas. A stylish crime epic with timeless performances, characters, vibes, and one hell of a score. 5 stars check it out 🇧🇷

Fantastic!  So many storylines.  So many characters.  All of them enhanced this movie. Nothing unnecessary. Nothing wasted.  It was captivating. And despite the tension building pace, all of the many characters were easy to connect to and the storylines were so easy to absorb. Beautifully shot.  So many techniques implemented.  But all with a purpose. Had this movie come out today with social media and streaming services, it would be massive. Maybe I underestimate its impact back in 2004, and it obviously garnered much critical acclaim, but I feel like a subtitled foreign film that probably wasn’t in a typical number of theaters and that you had to rent at the video store to be able to see, probably flew under most people’s radar.  It was certainly under mine. I cannot believe that I waited until 2026 to watch this masterpiece. 9.8/10

C’est définitivement un MOAT ( movie of all time ). J’avais des grandes attentes  envers ce film et il a livré la marchandise sur absolument tout les niveaux. C’était vraiment une belle expérience cinématographique, c’est un film si cru et vrai qui parle de la violence perpétuelle, mais qui trouve quand même le moyen de le faire de façon si belle et artistique. Les personnages sont intéressants les dialogues donne la sensation d’être présent dans une scène de la vrai vie et c’est ce qui fait tout le charme du film. Plusieurs plans magnifiques et une cinématographie incroyable accompagné d’une bande sonore qui agit comme une colle entre les éléments de cette fresque. J’ai adoré la façon dont l’histoire est racontée à travers les différentes perspectives et l’utilisation de la narration tout au long du film est vraiment unique et j’ai adoré. Absolute cinéma / 10

Okay this rambling of mine doesn’t make sense I’m warning you, I’m happy to have my mind changed. Very unpopular take, I think. Unfortunately, I probably was a bit too incapacitated for this movie, it did not click with me at all. I understand the intention of the long scenes and timed dialogue or actions but it was like I could hear a director in my head calling the cues for the characters, it unimmersed me frequently. Takabe also isn’t really showed to be burdened by his wife (what happened to in sickness and in health?), we don’t see the caretaker role in him at all, he just seeks a sort of liberation from social responsibility (looking after the person you love, who you made vows to). He feels burdened by the expectation that he should be a good partner to his wife, despite her becoming ill. We are not really shown the actual load that could be him having to look after her, the impact is detached and sterile (which thematically goes with the rest of the film) but his wife isn’t a true person, even in his story, she exists purely to illustrate his hardship . I’m sure I’ll attempt this movie again with a bit more respect, but for now my misandry hat has crept back on. Can’t even truely rate this movie upon this watch.

7/22/26 This movie leaves a lot to be desired. For one, there is almost no story to speak of. At the start of the movie we see that Mamiya can use supernatural powers to make people murder others. At the end of the movie we have no further clarification on that. We see the books, the video, and still we have no idea what is happening. Beyond just the lack of narrative there is a lack of character development. Mamiya does his bit the whole time and then dies. Takabe begins and ends the movie unable to control his emotions killing Mamiya. By the end of the movie I felt like I had just watched Seven, but vague. There was no one and nothing to really care about in the end. The thing I was most confused about were the reviews for this movie. It is not scary. There are a couple moments, but with the lack of sound it's never terrifying and it doesn't try to be. I also realized like with other movies the being vague is great for a movie. You can attribute as many things as you want to this film without ever being wrong.

this film did not work for me. the social commentary only really works, i think, if you bought into it ahead of time and are actively looking for it in the text. the (uncharismatic, irritating) hypnotist's victims aren't sufficiently fleshed out to support the idea that through subtle manipulation he's dredging up murderous misanthropic desires simmering beneath the surface of our alienated modern culture. it just looks like magic brainwashing. there's the implied horror, i suppose, of the fundamental unknowability of other people and even your own self, of what you are capable of thinking and doing under the right circumstances, but i just don't think the film actually conveys that in a compelling way. the first half drags. it's repetitive and kinda boring, showing the hypnotist's "method" over and over in a way that doesn't really build up to much. the second half is more entertaining to watch, but it's both too concrete to leave much up to interpretation and too abstract to set up and resolve the mystery, such as it was, in a satisfying way. the depiction of hypnosis stretched my suspension of disbelief thin, all in service of something that wasn't terrifying enough to instinctually scare or relatable enough to evoke a more conscious, intellectual dread. the film does some interesting stuff from a technical perspective, but that wasn't enough to hook me. tbh reading through the reviews i got the impression that either i watched a different film to everyone else, or the audience is 95% film students

The influences that contributed to this and also what came from it are very apparent, but unfortunately, this just did not work for me. I found it to be unbearably slow and uninteresting, and that’s coming from someone who often times appreciates a slower pace in film. What lost me on this was mainly the story; it was confusing and subtle in a way that the vagueness just made me continuously stay more and more unengaged as it went on. I found the character of Mamiya to be very frustrating and the long, drawn out scenes of his repetitiveness over and over again I really just disliked. I don’t know, I know a lot of people praise highly of this film and while I went in truly wanting to love it, I just never had that moment of connection. Kurosawa’s 2024 film “Chime” (which I was told was a spiritual successor this film) I think worked a lot better with its condensed runtime and modern filmmaking techniques. Although from a technical perspective, I found the production quality to be high and I also enjoyed the performances from the cast. This isn’t going to be something I revisit because I don’t see myself having a better experience but I’m glad those that get it, get it.

i liked the surrealism in certain scenes; felt like the movie was drifting in and out of the characters’ consciousness. the movie felt like it was in a fog, and that accurately represents the state most of the characters were in at times. i enjoyed the cinematography, sound, scenery, etc. there were direct nods to violence against women; a doctor carrying a lifetime of being told she’s not good enough to be one because of her gender, a murdered housewife institutionalized for mental strain because her life was shaped by the patriarchy/her “husband,” a woman murdered by yet another woman-hating man/“husband”, and.. you guessed it.. another woman murdered by a woman-hating man. lots of gender based violence being depicted, yet the focus of the movie is supposed to be two emotionally unstable men who obsess over one another and some mystical ability to hypnotize. i don’t have anything good to say about the premise of the villain’s hypnotism. the movie focused so much on this smoke screen instead of actually diving into the why behind violence (why men kill women). the villain felt too on the nose for me. the “mysterious” aspects of his character were repetitive and predictable after the first introduction to us. the theatrical nature of the villain kept creating a bigger and bigger disconnect between the violent themes of the movie that actually had something real and serious to explore. the feeling the villain and the detective evoked in me about 1/3 of the movie in was the same - there wasn’t really any differentiation between the two characters. the movie kept focusing on things that don’t have much substance (hypnotism, ambiguity, mystery, how the killer influences others, etc..) than focusing on the very real nature of male violence towards women and the psychological structure the patriarchy conditions both men and women into. there was something rich to explore here, but they missed the mark for me

This opens with a bang. It wastes no time at all ensnaring you in this whatthefuckery. The delightfully grimy atmosphere drips through every frame, and the lead performance is outstanding. But while both the lead performance and atmosphere never let up, the story ran out of steam after 40 minutes or so. Every conversation with the villain was the same conversation over and over again, and while it worked really well the first time, it got really repetitive and uninteresting after the 8th time. And by the time you get to the final act, the story really has nowhere to go except for where you expect it to. I love the bursts of violence, I love the cold drone that simmers on the soundtrack, and I think it’s occasionally pretty effective. But it’s more of a repetitive slog than anything else. I’m intrigued enough by it to want to read up about it a bit, so I guess that says something. I think it’s alright. It’s far from awful but it’s far from great either.

They don’t make sweaters like they used to. The primal urge to kill; just a flicker away. The terror of losing control and hurting the ones you love. The psychological as inseparable from the supernatural. Hypnotic, haunting, deeply unsettling. One of those movies that feels cursed to watch. Unfolds slowly, with a cold sense of inevitability. The assurance that you will snap someday; not a matter of ‘if’ but ‘when.’ The fire awakens something within you, an urge that has existed since the dawn of mankind. Maybe its influence is demonic in nature, maybe it’s baked into our DNA. A film too blackly intelligent to offer any easy answers or explanations; and besides, you know the truth anyway, don’t you? You’re just terrified to admit it to yourself. Kiyoshi Kurosawa is surely one of the best living writer-directors, a fact I am certain of even with this being my first film from him. A master of tone, pacing, storytelling; complete confidence in shot length, thematic subtlety, and a respect for the viewer to piece together information on their own. Beautiful, uneasy cinematography. Uses angles, windows, doorways, and distance to keep the viewer from the characters. You feel the urge to lean in, as if you’re an eavesdropper who just caught a glimpse of a strange conversation from across the beach. Long shots to prolong tension and deny release; to invite speculation, to sit with characters in moments of illogic and bewilderment. Koji Yakusho is one of the best living actors, full stop. He knows how to internalize his character’s emotions, convey changes in subtle ways, and go “big” and fully external when the story calls for it. Seeing him in a leading role is almost a seal of quality that the movie is going to be superb. This is not to discredit the work of his costars, whose work is on equal footing with his own, especially Masato Hagiwara, who gives one of the most skin-crawling performances I’ve ever seen in horror. As I was watching this, I didn’t want it to end. I know for a fact I’m going to rewatch this movie many times again, and I bet that I’ll get more out of it with each successive viewing. Its terrifying questions and insights into human psychology will stay with you long after the credits roll. This is unquestionably one of the greatest masterpieces in horror film history. Essential viewing. Mesmerizing.

Kurosawa lavora di pura sottrazione, appoggiandosi a un montaggio privo di sbavature e a interpretazioni di agghiacciante naturalezza per incollare lo spettatore allo schermo e mutarne radicalmente la prospettiva. Il vero orrore non risiede nell'ostentazione della violenza, ma nello spazio vuoto, in un gioco di luci e ombre gestito con l'autorità dei maestri. È un'opera che scava dritta nelle pulsioni più inconfessabili del nostro inconscio, lasciando un'impronta indelebile nell'immaginario di chiunque si esponga al suo sguardo. Un thriller psicologico ipnotico e viscerale, sconsigliato nelle ore notturne: la certezza che possa insinuarsi nella mente e non lasciarla più è fin troppo reale.

"All the things that used to be inside of me… now they are all outside." Kiyoshi Kurosawa’s Cure is one of the most quietly disturbing films ever made... an absolute masterpiece of psychological horror, existential dread, and suffocating restraint. On the surface it’s a serial‑killer procedural, even sharing DNA with Fincher’s brilliant Se7en, but Kurosawa uses the genre only as a skeleton. What he builds on top of it is a bleak, nihilistic examination of human vulnerability, the erosion of identity, and the terrifying idea that violence isn’t imposed from outside circumstance, but awakened from within. The story follows Detective Takabe (Kōji Yakusho), a man already stretched thin by his wife’s worsening mental illness and the emotional exhaustion of his job. His life is a fragile balancing act, and Kurosawa uses that instability as the perfect entry point for the film’s central horror: a series of murders committed by everyday ordinary people who have no motive, no memory, and no explanation. Their only connection is a wandering drifter named Mamiya (Masato Hagiwara), whose vacant stare and fragmented speech seem to hollow out the minds of everyone he encounters. Mamiya doesn’t kill... he just removes the part of people that resists killing. Kurosawa’s direction is astonishingly controlled. The pacing is glacial, the dialogue sparse, the atmosphere suffocating. Every scene feels slightly askew, as if reality itself is losing structural integrity. The cinematography is incredible: long static shots, oppressive negative space, and a washed‑out palette that makes Tokyo look like a decaying Silent Hill‑esque purgatory. Kurosawa weaponizes emptiness... rooms feel too large, hallways too long, silence too loud. The sound design is equally unnerving, filled with distant hums, mechanical drones, and the constant threat of nothing happening at all. It’s a film where the absence of action becomes the source of tension and dread. Yakusho’s performance is extraordinary. He plays Takabe with a brittle mix of intensity and (seeming) restraint... a man whose sense of self is eroding under the weight of responsibility and despair. His exhaustion becomes the emotional anchor of the film, making his slow descent into obsession and madness terrifying. Hagiwara’s Mamiya is the perfect counterpoint: airy, spacey, disturbingly serene. He’s not a villain in any traditional sense: he’s a void, a philosophical black hole that strips people down to their most primitive impulses. His presence evokes the same chilling inevitability as Anton Chigurh in No Country for Old Men, but filtered through a soft, almost childlike haze. The horror Kurosawa taps into feels even more potent today, where cycles of copycat violence (especially in the wake of high‑profile school shootings) show how fragile the boundary is between suggestion and action. Mamiya’s vacant presence unlocking buried impulses mirrors how real‑world perpetrators often inspire others not through ideology, but through a kind of psychological permission structure: the realization that someone else has crossed the line makes the line feel permeable. It’s deeply disturbing to recognize how prevalent violent urges are in humanity, how easily they can be awakened, and how quickly they spread when people see their own private darkness reflected in someone else’s public act. Cure forces us to confront the terrifying possibility that the capacity for violence is a dormant part of the human condition waiting for the right fracture. What makes Cure so remarkable is its refusal to offer answers. Kurosawa isn’t interested in explaining Mamiya’s methods or providing a neat psychological theory. Instead, he suggests something far more unsettling: that identity is fragile, morality is performative, and the boundary between self and suggestion is terrifyingly thin. The film becomes a meditation on how ordinary people justify extraordinary horrors, how violence blooms in the cracks of everyday life, and how the desire for meaning can lead to annihilation of self and others. It’s a worldview so depressingly bleak... and its quiet repression fits the late‑90s Japanese cultural landscape far more poignantly than the loud, chaotic spectacle of the modern American out-in-the-open bumfight/rainbet/pump.fun/Kalshi slop-filled attention economy. Cure works because it fuses philosophical horror, exquisite procedural mystery, and methodical atmospheric filmmaking into a hypnotic descent into existential terror. It’s deeply unsettling, thought‑provoking, and instantly one of the best films I’ve ever seen. Kurosawa understands that the violence lurking inside all of us (whether it ever emerges or not) is far scarier than any sort of monster or demon.

Difficile de réaliser que cette expérience se termine ! Dune a pompé toute ma joie, toute mon énergie tel un vers des sables. La seule chose notablement plaisante dans ce très long-métrage est ses plans : très jolis, beaux à voir. Bien que les costumes notamment bellement réalisés permettent de se projeter dans cet univers alternatif de fiction qu'est Dune . Malgré tout, ce film fut une torture et m'a renvoyé au jour qui avait déterminé le début de ma longue période de haine envers le cinéma. Sa lenteur, son écriture, son essence n'a pas grand chose à envier à Twilight , surtout au niveau du personnage principal. Pourtant, je suis surprise de le voir reconnu de façon différente que celui-ci ! Finalement, je préfère oublier cette expérience horriblement ennuyeuse (et ennuyante) — même si cela me sera difficile.

There are two overlapping narrative strands, the conflict between houses and Paul becoming acquainted with (/returning to??) the ways of the desert. I was ever so slightly disappointed with the swift buildup and resolve of the former. In the end, the imperial betrayal and setup of House Atreides was merely expositional, functional for the Lisan al-Gaib pipeline which this trilogy is clearly going to be “about.” I’m told that’s how they do franchises these days, but something about watching a nearly three hour long (and brilliant!) film only to have it end with “there will be a second one!!!” in big bright neon letters irritated me. In a way, the semi-forced cliffhanger ending undermined the  value of the otherwise very intriguing world-building, at least for me.  Lastly, I couldn’t help but cringe a bit at Chalamat’s Daenerys-moment in the desert

Excellent cinematography and direction…however, this has to be one of the slowest and dullest movies I’ve ever watched for a franchise of this size. It’s easy to see why this story was long considered unadaptable for the big screen. The film has the difficult task of introducing multiple families, political factions, key locations, religious themes, and complex world-building, all of which are challenging to translate from the novel to film. Denis deserves credit for making such a dense and difficult story coherent, but I don’t think the pacing works. I understand that much of the film is dedicated to laying the groundwork for the sequels, but watching it often felt more like homework than an engaging introduction to this world. I admire the craftsmanship far more than I enjoyed the experience. 3/5

Do you think the worms would be snuggly? They are very cute! The main theme for this is so heavenly. Gives me chills. I absolutely love it. I love Hans Zimmer. But I think recently he hasn’t been at his greatest. He’s made masterpieces of scores, like Interstellar and Inception. But Dunkirk just was bad , Top Gun: Maverick score didn’t feel special, F1 score also didn’t feel special at all. But the score for this, amazing. Masterpiece. Okay, the cinematography is good, but not great. The first 20 minutes I was thinking that the cinematography was amazing. But after that it just went from “this looks good” at certain scenes and that’s it. I mean it just all looks the same. It’s all orange. Dusty orange. They did really amazing shots with it though, don’t get me wrong. But the cinematography was a let down because so many people say “This has one of the best cinematography of all time!” Spider-Man: Brand New Day had better cinematography than this. It’s great. I really enjoyed it. It’s a bang average 4 star film. It’s an amazing set up for what’s coming next. But that’s an issue to be honest. My only two issues was the cinematography was kinda disappointing and this just feels like a set up film. Don’t get me wrong, I really enjoyed this, setup film or not. But I’m hardly ever a fan of those. Especially risky if you don’t know that you could make a sequel. Luckily, Denis did make that sequel and the third and final one is coming out in December. So I can breathe easily. Like I said, I was really enjoying it. But since it’s so long and the school year just started so I’m tried as hell. Literally right after the 2 hour mark I started like dozing off. Not because I was bored, far from that, but just really tired. I would wake up like 5 seconds after so I didn’t miss anything, only happened like 5 times. I have a love and hate relationship with long films. I love when they are usually a solo film, but something like this makes me nervous (with multiple other films.) Because I enjoyed it and will watch the second one and third one in theaters. But just really don’t want to watch the second one because it’s much longer. I have time before December so I’ll watch it eventually. But I doubt this month or next month. But I will! I want to write more but I’m just too damn tired.. I did it guys, I finally watched Dune!

Denis Villeneuve has delivered a masterpiece. From the opening scenes, you're completely transported to the harsh, breathtaking world of Arrakis. The cinematography is next-level-those sweeping desert shots and massive sandworms left me speechless. Timothée Chalamet nails Paul Atreides' inner conflict with quiet intensity, while Rebecca Ferguson, Oscar Isaac, and Zendaya bring so much depth to their roles. The sound design and Hans Zimmer's thundering score hit you in the chest. It's a slow, deliberate build that respects the source material without rushing. Not everyone will love the pacing, but for book fans like me, this is pure cinematic joy.

I tried watching this once before and gave up like 12 minutes in because I was confused and bored. Turns out I just needed to let the movie cook. The world building here is fucking insane. I loved the politics between the different houses and how each one has its own identity, while Paul’s destiny slowly develops in the background. The movie doesn’t rush to explain everything either; it lets you be confused sometimes and gives you the answers later. I’m especially interested in seeing what Paul becomes because you can already feel how much potential and power he has. But I wasn’t nearly as invested in most of the characters. Besides Paul, Jessica and Chani, a lot of them felt disposable. Duncan was one of the few supporting characters I actually liked and then they got rid of him way too easily. Some of the dialogue also felt forced, especially when Paul started saying some of the weirder shit. Production-wise though, holy shit. The production design is insane. The ships, architecture, costumes and scale make this universe actually feel massive. Villeneuve’s wide shots aren’t just there to look pretty either; Arrakis and the desert tell you things about this world without anyone having to say a word. The large-scale scenes are incredible, the sound design is powerful, and even though some effects like the shields could’ve looked better, visually this movie is ridiculous. And Hans Zimmer… this would genuinely be a different movie without him. The score gives so much power to the world and makes the slower pace work incredibly well. It’s definitely slow, but once I understood that this is the beginning of a much bigger story, I stopped caring about the runtime. Instead of finishing it bored like I expected, I finished it curious as fuck to see where this story and Paul go next.

“That's the future. It's coming. Holy war spreading across the universe like unquenchable fire.” A young and vulnerable Paul is introduced to what his future holds through his visions, war, violence and tragedy. Despite what he sees he has no choice but to find the Fremens in order to survive on Arakis even though this will kickstart his controversial Messiah arc. Remarkable way to set the scene for part two, leaving us with the perfect point to pick up from. The world building and character development is also fantastic. First time rewatching part one and I can definitely appreciate a lot this time around now that I know a lot more about the Dune lore in general. Really one of them films that just gets more epic the more you begin to deep it. Can’t wait for a the Christmas Dune aesthetic later this year, can already feel how nostalgic it will be in years to come.

Somehow Dune: Part Two managed to be even longer, louder, and somehow still feel like nothing was happening. In the first film, Paul Atreides was treated like a legendary figure before I ever understood why I should care about him. Unfortunately, Part Two doubles down on that. Everyone keeps looking at Paul like he’s the greatest thing to ever walk across the desert, but the movie never really earns that feeling. We’re constantly told he’s a messiah or the chosen one but I’m still waiting for the part where I understand why. Instead of watching a character become extraordinary, it feels like watching everyone else convince themselves that he already is. The Fremen’s devotion to Paul also made the story harder to take seriously. It feels less like a believable movement and more like an entire population suddenly joining a religion because the script told them to. And the final was strangely underwhelming. A story that spends so much time preparing for greatness somehow ends on a very ordinary note. Two movies, almost five hours, and my main takeaway is still: more sand, more silence, more people telling me Paul is special.

I think this is the greatest example of a “good” movie vs. an “enjoyable/favorite” movie I’ve ever seen. I say that because this movie is GREAT from nearly all technical standpoints. Great actors doing some great acting, absolutely beautiful cinematography and special effects, insanely impressive sets, and just a sheer feeling of grandness that, I feel, is only topped by a handful of movies. All around, just a beautifully made film. Still, I didn’t enjoy myself AT ALL. I don’t think the story is nearly as impressive as the first one, or impressive at all for that matter. I find it boring, confusing, and just honestly dull. I find that they waste unreasonable amounts of time on storylines that don’t matter and/or just aren’t entertaining, and rush the very few things I actually enjoyed. I mean, and this is obviously the card they were dealt, seeing as this was based on a book, it’s all just talking and politics, but they do it so different in this land, “Arakkis,” that half the film is spent explaining all of that through boring exposition and whatnot, and the other half is not very interesting at all, as someone who enjoys stories similar to this, like Game of Thrones. The action scenes, though VERY far and few were, again, gorgeously and impressively shot, but I feel lack stakes, substance, and, again, enjoyment. Half of the scenes just felt like Neo and Agent Smith going at it, even though Neo already knows all of the moves Agent Smith will make. This was a dumb comparison, in hindsight, but what I mean to say is that they’re un-compelling and boring for the most part, besides that gladiator-type fight in the middle and the fight scene with the big tank thing near the 40-minute mark. The characters- don’t get me started on the characters. I’m guessing this is something most people actually LIKE about Dune- seeing as they are able as realistic of characters you can write given their positions, but I sincerely couldn’t name you one that I care about/ like. I mean, in the first one, I cared about Paul because he actually had a personality, I liked Jason Momoa’s character a lot, and I thought the Baron was a very intriguing villain, but this time around, there was none of that charm. Everyone was just this boring, dull, character with seemingly the same personality, unless you’re Paul or his mother, because then you have NO personality, making the finale and all of the stuff with Chani pretty uninteresting and unrewarding to be quite honest. Again; the fact that this movie even got to be made is a wonder within itself- with all of those spacecrafts, settings, character designs, buildings, etc, that they had to create, shoot, and put to film is such a tasteful way, but I just didn’t enjoy it at all. I found it to be INSANELY long, like, blood-curdlingly long in my opinion, to the point where I was just actually started to breathe heavier (coming from someone who likes longer movies) and (with zero exaggeration whatsoever) probably checked how much longer it was roughly 15-20 times, very boring and dull, lifeless if you will, and everything I “liked” about it wasn’t done any better than what I’ve seen a gazillion times before. My rating: 3.4/10

I watched this movie right when it came out because I’m friends with this nerd who loves Dune. He’s read the books and everything, the books actually lose the plot after like the 3rd one according to him. For example the grandson of Paul (who is the main character further down the line) is actually just one of those sand worms, no human part he’s a sand worm and somehow that works I suppose. Anyways why did I give this a 2? Well there’s a few reasons. First I should mention I slammed 2 Four Lokos during the runtime of this movie, which got me pretty loko ngl. In fact I blacked out at some point during the film and spawned back in at the final fight. But before that happened I felt the movie was too slow and convoluted. My very informed opinion was backed up because my friend said the books do a much better job of explaining what’s going on and it’s hard to explain it visually which is what the movie has to do. Also he had to explain the movie to everyone we watched it with (they did not have Four Lokos, they were sober) because even they had no idea what was going on, and there were a bunch of unexplained scenes that you can only understand if you read the book. For example they’ll flash a scene with Anya Taylor Joy and you’re gonna be like wtf, but since we had a guide he told us that’s his sister and his moms race can see shit or something? Idk, I don’t remember but I think you get the point. Luckily he was our guide. You need to watch this movie with a guide or you’re just gonna be watching people hanging out in the sand. However I do not think this movie is bad, it’s well made. Very visually interesting despite the fact that it’s just sand, and the characters are interesting, the mystery is interesting. It’s also not poorly paced, it just felt slow for my taste. What brings it down to a 2 is that you basically either have to read the books or watch a YouTube video to understand what’s going on and in my opinion that is a film that doesn’t do its job well. If you can’t understand the story from watching the movie then it failed. I believe it has failed a bit as a film, but it’s quality saves it hence the slightly below average rating. TLDR: Watch it off of 2 Four Lokos because you’re not gonna understand what’s going on anyways.

Dune annoyed me during this viewing, and it falls off each time I watch it. Let's call this the " Endgame paradigm", and blame my excising liberalism. I'd like to make three points, or point out three categories which I see as quite deficient. Firstly: Fremen Denis elects for a blankly Afro-Asiatic look for the Fremen, making them a simultaneously sub-Saharan, Middle-eastern, and North African people. Nevermind that they have been an isolated population with nye-on zero outside inter-mingling possible. He also chooses to include death wailing in the grieving of Jamis. This genero-ethnic mix betrays the desire to vaguely represent all of the (virtuous) third world in the Fremen, and to marry this minted people with Islam. It berays the portrayal into a more favourable framing than that of Frank Herbert, and complicates the story with a more cosmopolitan, pluralist appearance than was given them by their creator. Denis wants the residents of Arrakis to be somewhat blameless in their behaviour and sympathetic in their desires, even if they are implied to be stupid by following Paul. Yes, this is a backwards culture, but it is one that Denis seems to simultaneously revere and chide. This is a problem for many modern liberals, who would love to totally embrace Islam and Islamists, but can’t quite get over their pesky superstition. Attila and the witch doctor. Second: Method As has become an assumption of modern production, handheld, mid-close shots with a shallow depth-of-field obfuscate the production elements in the background. The reflecting pool with Stilgar and Jessica is a good example. What is the point of all of the beautiful and very detailed work of set production if we cannot see it? This method also subverts the style of the sci-fi/warfare epic we know - work of the likes of David Lean - which is a fine stylistic choice in a vacuum, surely, but aggravating when it seems to genuinely lessen the feature. Where are our grand wide shots in 65mm? They disappeared by taste, and have not returned because of our self-importance and our view of method as a continuum from which we would be foolish to get off. As a result, I dislike much of how the film was shot. Opening with such a stylized eclipse scene does the rest of the film no favours. "Realism" apparently means no lighting or blocking work in most shots. That might also have something to do with the fact that most shots are CG, or contain CG composites. The very effective scenes (like hunting Harkonnen in the sandstorm ) make you wonder how much more effective they might have been with better lighting. And there are tons of lens flares here like would get Zach Snyder made fun of, but I have heard nothing of them. So I don't think I like Greig Fraser. Third: Meaning The movie thematically leans deeper into the commentary and critique of the novel, and does so inelegantly. With every modern auteur who claims themselves a "realist" whose joy it is to approximate reality, there is this kind of inelegance and incoherency which pervades their films. (For example: in fidelity to the faith, all Hollywood productions are now pluralist and cosmopolitan after the manner of the creators' experience walking down the street, regardless of their diegetic setting.) Despite Frank Herbert’s principal antagonist in this analogy, Dune the Movie's religious critique is more directed at Christianity than it is Islam. The local religion of the Arrakeans (more analogous of Islam, and more sympathetic) is subservient to the misanthropic political calculation of the Bene Gesserit, who themselves firmly believe in a messiah figure, but one of their own making; they believe that they can conjure his coming. Ultimately, his arrival is so great and terrible as none of them could have foreseen, and though the religious leaders are put off of his upending and (yet) fulfilling their prophecy, they are eventually powerless to do anything about the rise of the faith of Lisan al Ga'ib, or of the number of his adherents. We the audience are given an anachronism in Chani and the disbelieving secularists for our point-of-view character, and Denis ensures that they make all the right assertions. Excepting, of course, that assertive question or two which could cause Paul pause... From whence are these dreams coming? Obviously, the story parallels better with the advent of Christ to the upheaval of the Jewish legalists and fulfillment of their prophecy, and so this portion of the film plays a bit like historical fan fiction, wherein the atheist of today gets to go back and ask his brilliant and cutting questions of Jesus of Nazareth. He, of course, can see right through the religious deception. From all of this modernist compulsion to the "realism" of our day, and a compunction against representing women, minorities, or, indeed, rational (unreligious) people badly (or at least, without excusing them by trauma or manipulation from their bad behaviour), the film's immersion strains. The anachronism of a complete lack of belief from Chani and the secularists is one of the first inflection points. (The secular Fremen are a somewhat large and vocal number in the film, enough to make the distinction of the "southern fundamentalists" a relevant one, even if not subtle.) Chani will talk both in the novel and these movies as a believer of something. Across the mediums, one can hear her - say that Shai-hulud is sacred, especially in his role in the production of spice, - assert that water and the burial rites are important in a spiritual, and not just practical sense, - say that spice is her people's birthright, and - talk of her son, and of her husband's prodigious sister providentially (as though some force brought each to them). Chani's assassination in this film (a wholly different character than the novel, and self-contradictory in the movies themselves) happens to bring her from adapted character, to one with the same thoroughly modern opinion of religion as the writers. Imagine that. And so, with this self-portrait of Denis, we are left to conclude that more than an audience-insert with whom we are meant to sympathize (and by whom we transpose ourselves into the story), Chani is intended as a theme and message delivering bullhorn -- a manner by which the writers might tell you what the story is about. Which is how we get lines like, "You wanna control people? You tell them a messiah will come, then they wait for centuries." More than just a thematic narrator, she is the writer’s holy self-insert, for where Paul is in agreement with Chani, deriving his understanding of the world through her, he is in the right. Only when he begins to reject her framing, making use of his power and of the religious fervour of the Fremen, does he begin to be wrong. "What your people did to this world is heartbreaking." - "We gave them something to hope for." - "That's not hope!" contrasted with “I am pointing the way! (…) God be my witness: I am the Lisan al-Gaib. I will lead you to paradise!” In Denis’ movie, a character's proximity to the masculine political tendencies (exercising direct authority, reacting aggressively when faced with hostility, viewing war as a political solution, et al.), and, more crucially, their proximity to the religious determines their quality. The feminist and anti-Christian sentiment in the film was inevitable, the outworking of Herbert’s own framing, and of Denis and the writers writing what they know: they weigh every (white) man, colonial effort, and every Christian, and find them wanting. It makes their job easier that conflating these is something that we already do, as history’s colonial efforts were often white and Christian. And Herbert gives the modern creator many excuses for woman worship in particular. Setting quite the bar for inelegance already, the Chani character being made a cudgel for the writer to beat the viewer about the ears with the right interpretation of things is somehow not an assassination so severe as that of Stilgar. His character turned into a joke as he was is not appropriate to the tone, nor useful to the theme. In so doing, the writers sabotage his contributions to Paul's own "conversion" to his myth. It takes the teeth out of the line, "I don't care what you believe! I believe!" if we are constantly jeering at the silliness of faith. A driving component of Frank Herbert’s work was to show the signs and wonders of Paul as a genuinely compelling, insidious deception. Gawking at the silliness of faith and prophecy constantly does not help us to find the myth compelling, especially when the character who is meant to represent sincere faith to us as a cautionary warning is the one at whom we have been laughing. Additionally, Denis in his secular modernism cannot resist giving everything a science-y explanation, leaving nothing but the visions to the spiritual, with even those receiving a handwave as, "planted by the Bene Gesserit." (That is the best explanation as given by the book, near as I can remember, but the impression is given in the film that it is some kind of device – whether psychological or technological – that has achieved this, and that this inception is not even done by a spiritual means. Meaning that the Bene Gesserit have a closer relation in Villeneuve to Scientology and hypnotists than they do any of the Christian tradition.) The mystery of the spiritual force at work in the events of this universe is part of the compelling nature of the narrative. Who or what force is at work in these events? Is this messiah who can see the future really possible, and is it really Paul? Even if we rug-pull all of the spiritual elements at the last minute for the big reveal that it was the Order all along, there would be a more convincing conniving and malevolent quality to Paul’s works, which better sells the theme. We are meant to come away from this tale feeling cautiously inward, wondering where we have been the victim of religious propaganda, or how we might have been carried off by soaring rhetoric and religious zealotry. Did anyone walk away from the movie Dune: Part Two thinking that they had seen a serious critique of religion? Did anyone walk out with that worry that they too would have been swept up in Paul’s ascendency if they were one of the Fremen? In all the confusing rhetoric of the film, the point is that you, audience member, would have something to latch on to. The strategy is shotgun vagary: there’s something in it for everyone. Just as the casting means there's someone in it for everyone. With the first Dune , I had a hope that there was a resurgence of questions about faith and fate in film. Blade Runner 's moral clarity made me even more hopeful as to Villeneuve's chances with Paul. Unfortunately, he is evidently still an atheist. Dune: Part Two is, however (as I often caveat movies, and for your sake, dear reader), in portions, very fun to watch. While I have more to say about the technique of the film, I have probably reached your limit, haven't I? I know I have reached my own. 50/100

(Written in 2026) So, after 2 years of reflection (more like 10 months but shhhh), I've come to the realization that Dune: Part Two is overrated. This film contains very little of what I enjoyed about the first film, and it's so generally unimpressive that its flimsy narrative takes center stage. Gone are the complex politics of Dune and its varied and complex scenery, insert a rehash of the already lackluster score of the first film, and a lack of technical flair from every department, and you get this film. The cast is fine, although generally weaker than in the first film. The cinematography and sound are still good (although less impressive than Dune ), but the production design is too bland, and Fraser's insistence on using mostly wide/extra wide shots showing mostly empty scenery doesn't hide the production design flaws. The editing is also notably worse here, Denis Villeneuve/Joe Walker remain insistent to linger on certain shots for too long, once again grinding the pace to a complete halt, and wringing out whatever energy the viewer has left. Back to the cast, Austin Butler is a very disappointing Feyd-Rautha. He does a uniquely awful job at instilling fear (what with his on-again/off-again Elvis accent ruining whatever was left of the dialogue), which betrays the work he put in on the combat choreography. He also lacks any real skill physicality-wise, all of the random yells, spasms, and "quirks" of his performance come off as comedic and are totally unfit for the character's role in the film. The action sequences in the film are also no longer the strength they were in the first film, with Villeneuve's staging and Frasier's cinematography becoming progressively less interesting throughout the film.

Visuellement bluffant, émotionnellement creux. Aie Aie Aie. Je m'attendais à BEAUCOUP mieux que la partie 1, mais à peine. Toutefois, les raisons de mon retrait sont différentes entre la partie 1 et la partie 2. À de nombreuses reprises, j'ai trouvé le film austère et glacial avec un manque de liens émotionnels avec les personnages. Par exemple, j'aurais aimé voir comment Chani et Paul se sont rapprochés car au départ elle avait quand même des doutes et lui avait ses visions prémonitoires la concernant. Enfaite, j'ai trouvé leur rapprochement hyper soudain comme précipité tout en étant assumé et c'est pas pour moi. De manière générale, je sens une certaine précipitation des évènements de la part de Villeneuve, ce qui m'a fait décroché. Des années ont l'air de passer comme des semaines là où, je peux le sentir, les livres doivent probablement bien nous le faire sentir ce temps qui passe. Autre remarque, l'expansion et la croissance de la "religion" de la mère de Paul qui est fourré au 1000e plan du film. J'aurais aimé un focus dessus parce qu'une parole de la mère qui dit "il faut commencer par ceux qui ont peurs" et puis "on a fini avec le nord, passons au sud"... mouais Denis steuplait hein. Des révélations chocs comme le fait que la mère de Paul soit la fille du baron et la mort symbolique de celui-ci part la main de son petit-fils m'ont laissé de marbre. Je soupçonne que cela s'explique par, pour moi encore une fois, un retrait de l'intrigue politique au second plan afin de polluer le premier plan du film sur le fait que tout indique que Paul est le Lisan Al-Ghaib (jeu de mot qui m'a fait croire à autre chose et je pense que c'était totalement le but). Je ne dis pas qu'il n'y a aucune intrigue politique, ce serait mentir sans vergogne. Je dis plutôt que sa place est hybride là où elle devrait être centrale. Toutefois, je comprendrais que d'autres ne pensent la même chose, et c'est OK. On retrouve des personnages qui se veulent être impactant retirer de tout leur éclat dû à un manque de place affligeant (ex: Empereur, Rautha). J'ai également du mal à croire en la relation entre Paul et sa mère. Leurs interactions me font plus penser à un frère et sa soeur plutôt qu'à un fils et sa mère. Vers la fin elle se reprend mais bon. Si on recentre notre attention sur Paul, j'ai pas compris en quoi c'était évident qu'il aille chercher la potion bleue. Pour moi c'est un peu sorti de nulle part. Oui oui sa prescience etc mais je suis pas convaincu par ce que je vois, justement parce que tout va vite et de manière très déconnecté. Et son shift ne s'explique pas tant que ça, on peut le comprendre en l'imaginant mais ce n'est jamais rien de factuel là où on comprenait celui d'Anakin par exemple. D'ailleurs, on sent que ce film est un film qui prépare le prochain. Ça m'a un peu dérangé. mais ça reste minime. Passons au positif, c'est déprimant sinon. J'ai beaucoup aimé le choix visuel de passer de la couleur au noir et blanc dans l'arène. Je n'ai pas d'explication au phénomène mais c'était sympa. De plus, les éléments du film sont présents mais mal intégré à mon avis, c'est dommage. (pff j'étais censé virer au positif) L'amourette bien que rapide est mignonne. On peut imaginer que Paul et Chani tienne énormément l'un à l'autre. De plus, j'ai bien aimé la première traversée du désert de Paul avec Chani. Les plans étaient beaux, l'ambiance était chic, les chorégraphies étaient apaisantes par leur synchronicité. Bref c'était chouette. Enfin, j'aime bien l'idée d'un faux saveur qui s'approprie les mythes pour parvenir à ses fins. C'est intéressant. On en vient même à se demander si le mythe est réellement faux ou s'il est devenu réel à force de le propager ou s'il a toujours été réel. Notre avis peut néanmoins se trouver biaisé par la mise en scène et le pdv de Paul (visions etc). Bref, c'est sympa ça. PS: Voir les idées des adaptations m'a donné envie de débuter les livres un jour. J'pense que j'apprécierai plus. Ou bien pas du tout et ça conclura ma tentative désespérée :( PS2: Niveau religion, et ce que traduit cette oeuvre, je préfère me taire sinon j'vais écrire 3 pavés supplémentaires. Pas content. Frank Herbert est un cas mais Denis Villeneuve est tout aussi en faute pour l'image qu'il renvoie. PS3: Je pense sincèrement qu'une série aurait été plus adaptée pour cette oeuvre.

3 stars only because I love the book so much and enjoy watching it come to screen. Too many things have been squeezed into this film, it covers such a large period of time as well as squeezing in the details about the Harkonens that happen in the first part of the story in the book that aren't included in the first film. Consequently, this film feels like a series of events strung together with little impact when major items happen. Many of the character motivations and personalities are also changed, some for the better (like Chani who frankly has no personality in the books) and some for the worse (Stilgar and Lady Jessica). Because of all of this, I also don't really believe in Chani and Paul's romance in this film, we're given no time to see an actual relationship blossom, we're just told through a montage and time jump that they're together. And Timothee Chalamet and Zendaya have no chemistry. Highlights of the film include Austin Butler's Feyd-Rauther, which he plays brilliantly, and the amazing cinematography (which at times feels a little excessively self-indulgent and doesn't necessarily blend with the rest of the film (Geidi Primes)).

Interested to see what happens with Paul’s character in the third movie, but I assume it’ll follow the book and he becomes somewhat of an evil character. If so, it will be realistic but obviously not the happy ending people would want.

Dune 2; Harkonnen Boogaloo The production on these movies continues to blow me away.  It feels like watching something from Moebius or Druillet in live action.  The costumes, the music, the differences in the worlds, heck even the language is all so well done that it feels both alien and completely natural all at the same time. I also really loved the looks of all of the Harkonnen machines.  One of the things that Villeneuve and the crew here have done very well across both films is give a sense of the weight and physics of these things.  The giant worms, the miners, the crashed ornithopters.  They all have very believable weight to them.  I've seen several bad sci-fi films where they forget about that in the fx.  They'll have these giant machines that look like they are walking across rice paper without damaging it. Watching these movies gives me the same sort of feeling that I got when I was watching The Lord of the Rings for the first time.
