I’m still yet to see The Odyssey, but it’s basically impossible to read anything related to film right now and not find an essay on how Christoper Nolan has finally completed his accidental reverse  triptych on tracing the evolution of man's relationship to power and evil, on the heroes who mistake intelligence for virtue. The Odyssey imagines the mythic birth of strategic violence, to be cunning is to acquire the status of a moral good. Tenet imagines something much later and much more bleak, the bureaucratisation of the apocalypse. While Oppenheimer is found somewhere in the middle, the shift from strategy to science, the genius who acquires the capacity to destroy the world. History, read backwards, starts to echo a series of increasingly sophisticated excuses of exceptional men. It’s a very stylish and neat way to view the films, more stylish and neat, perhaps, then the films themselves. And while these film’s three leads, Odysseus, Oppenheimer, and the Protagonist may be from different centuries, experiencing different crises, each man crosses a threshold that cannot be uncrossed, each inheriting history itself as both burden and the very justification for existence.  And I don’t know if I fully agree, Nolan doesn’t quite seem the type of filmmaker to spend over a decade silently remaking the same film; but the reading makes one thing feel clear to me, that Oppenheimer is much more a clear symptom of Nolan’s work than his masterpiece. I’m not exactly a fan of Tenet, a film less intellectually rigorous than hermetically sealed, so completely fascinated by its own narrative mechanisms, smugly constructing its timeloop as an axiom, that it never stops to ask if it is mistaking opacity for complexity. For a film that is supposed to feel like human agency is being dissolved into infrastructure, it’s strangely legible, the end was always written into the beginning, it all makes sense in the end, there’s always a hero to its story, even if we only see the consequences of actions already chosen. If I wanted cinema like that then I’d much rather take Assayas’s Demonlover, or Denis’s Bastards every time, at least those films see something Nolan never can bring into sight; those systems become frightening because no one can comprehend them. The very forms of those films do not ask us to admire their architectures, but they ask us to live inside the consequences, never becoming legible because the modern world does not allow for it; these are stories of networks, not heroes. But with Oppenheimer I find my feelings more disjointed; it doesn’t help that the public reaction to the film seems to proclaim it as the grand brilliant masterpiece to define the 2020s American cinema. It’s obviously an accomplished film on most technical levels, and I can appreciate a lot of it’s editing, and a genuine fantastic lead performance; but any admiration I have turns to stone by the time its greatest irony has come to light; a film about the invention of systems capacity of escaping our control (nuclear winter) is so convinced that history is driven by the great man. How can one singular consciousness make us feel the weight of such horrors? The Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings show up not as straight realities but as subjective events that disturb Oppenheimer’s own interior life. Is the film refusal to depict these events an ethical one to stop atrocity turning into aesthetics? I’m not convinced, we leave so much knowing about what it feels to invent the bomb, but we feel so little about what that means for… everyone else, including those who lived beneath it. The limits of making a biopic about a man’s guilt is failing to be a statement on how humanity doomed itself with his invention, you either make us understand catastrophe, or how it feels to be ‘great’ but ‘cursed’. Nolan’s films have always been fascinated by guilt, exceptional men have to be crushed eventually by the weight of their exceptional decisions, too heavy for ‘normal people’ to understand; but guilt is not morality, and Nolan’s guilt more resembles proof of one’s exceptional depth than functioning as their own ethical reckoning. Oppenheimer must suffer so intensely through his mind that his suffering becomes the film’s moral inquiry. Are we ‘really’ confronting evil? Or just watching a man’s conscience work as usual? (I feel like those TikToks about men where it’s like ‘men are just now having the thoughts we have at a sleepover at nine’). Again and again, in Nolan’s cinema, civilisation persists because one extraordinary man discovers that one’s intelligence can allow them to suspend morality. Splitting the atom, the Trojan Horse, controlling time itself. Different myths that share the fundamental conviction, history depends on the men who act when everyone else cannot. But that’s the rancid conservative impulse at the heart of his filmmaking, maybe not quite in the partisan sense (although we’ve all seen the think pieces on Dark Knight and Interstellar), but in the shape of his histories. This nineteenth century imagination being recycled back into contemporary culture, a world now ruled by invisible systems and anonymous power, it’s ironically, a very romantic vision of a lost past disguised as modernity. Carlyle’s influence is exhausting, the ending of two geniuses talking about the future of the nuclear age might be even worse. Don’t forget, it was a Nazi who said that sovereignty is revealed in the exception, Nolan might as well endorse it through his fantasies. Of course, there is an obvious objection to my claims, Odysseus devises the Horse; the Protagonist orchestrates events from both ends of time, but Oppenheimer doesn’t drop the bomb, he just invents it. Power has already migrated elsewhere; into the invisible machinery of Cold War America. The point isn’t that Oppenheimer controls history, it’s that Nolan insists on making him the center of it. The film shows that history’s decisive moral drama is located at the moment of invention, not administration. As if Oppenheimer becomes the last individual capable of containing this history with any moral imagination, the bomb no longer belongs to him, but the film behaves as if the bomb’s only meaning does. However history does not have a centre, catastrophe cannot be understood through the conscience of one man, however remarkable they might have been. Oppenheimer mistakes the scale of its subject for the depth of its thought. This perhaps explains why I left Oppenheimer remaining untouched by its very indifferent ideas on the means of humanity’s own destruction. Nolan wants to imagine a world transformed by things too powerful for any one individual to contain. But his imagination cannot stop returning to the individual who started it all, however powerless they might be. A filmmaker who dreams of networks but still believes in heroes that even his tragedies preserve the mythology of exceptional men. That might have worked for the Greeks, but it works less for the bomb.

Oppenheimer est symptomatique de la filmographie de Cristopher Nolan. Il réinterprète des sujets passionnants et complexes avec des moyens colossaux et une capacité rare de créer un engouement massif auprès du grand public. Cependant, Oppenheimer, tout comme Interstellar ou Tenet, tombe toujours dans les mêmes travers qui font de ses œuvres des gâchis bien tristes. Des temporalités mélangées, où on aime faire des bonds dans le futur pour inlassablement revenir en arrière, des twists de merde artificiellement complexifiés et des personnages qui aiment s'écouter parler. Un cinéma "intelligent" ou un cinéma balourd qui impose à son public de se concentrer pendant 3 heures jusqu'à ne plus rien comprendre tant on est surchargés d'information pour se convaincre de la supériorité cérébrale de son scénario. Volontairement fatiguant, rien n'est développé si sa mise en scène ne sert pas l'histoire, le film passe son temps à expliquer ce qu'il ne filme pas. On apprend pas grand chose de Oppenheimer, de ce qu'il est, de ce qu'il fait, de ce qu'il le motive, de l'homme de science qu'il a été, de l'homme de pouvoir qu'il est devenu, de ses états d'âme, des conséquences de ses actions. Mais on préfère s'étendre sur un procès qui se passe on ne sait pas trop quand exactement, parce que Robert Downey Jr. est on se sait pas trop qui, qui souhaite empêcher à Cilian Murphy on ne sait pas trop quoi qui permettrait à ce dernier de faire quelque chose de sûrement important. Et c'est pas le film qui va nous aider à y voir beaucoup plus clair, profitant de la confusion pour mieux cacher les lacunes de Nolan. Au final, on finit par s'extasier sur le moindre acteur un peu connu ou sur des scènes bien américaines comme le namedrop de JFK vers la fin du film comme si c'était une scène post crédit Marvel. Mais peut-être que les histoires de cul intéressent plus Nolan que le tragique des bombardements atomiques d'Hiroshima et de Nagasaki dont tout semblait faux (et ce n'est pas la faute à Cilian Murphy) puisque le film n'avait cœur à rien. Spectacle du rien, psychologie de comptoir. Politiquement inconséquent, gâchis complet pour un film qui aurait mérité d'être plus digeste si Nolan ne faisait pas tout pour plomber sa mise en scène.

i'm gonna preface this with a warning that i've grown very disillusioned with christopher nolan as of late. i haven't lost affection for his films of which i am already fond, but i am a lot more aware of his shortcomings as a director now than i have historically been, and they bother me a lot more. honestly sometimes with all the glazing going on i feel like film enjoyers are under some kind of group psychosis about how talented the man is. buuuuut that is neither here nor there, because today i am here to talk about oppenheimer . i think i had a decently open mind going in, and the film got off to a good start. i mean, the thing hauls. from the very beginning, something is always happening. it left me feeling breathless, but eventually i realized it was not in a good way. it kinda just made me tired. i would've been impressed if it had maintained the momentum all the way through, but the endless repetition of "important" conversation after important conversation got old and then the momentum didn't matter anymore. each conversation felt like an event that needed to happen before the story could move along to the next. a sequence of interactions, each ending with a miniature mic-drop, that communicated information but didn't say anything interesting. i took a note that compared this constant vapid go-go-go to my own tendency to play music 24/7 to distract myself from everything, including and especially my own interiority. i know it's an unfulfilling and terribly un-present way to live, but it avoids most discomfort. this film is largely the same! rapid pace & perpetual talking unsuccessfully try to distract from the fact that nothing weighty is being discussed. we're talking about the invention & use of the atomic bomb, for fricks sake, and i basically just dissociated under the impression of a meaningful movie for three hours. there are a couple scenes that made me think it was about to pivot in a more interesting & resonant direction—the meeting to decide if/where to drop the bombs on japan (perfectly sickening), and the conference with oppenheimer speaking to los alamos about the bombs' "performance", to name two—but then we were right back in a series of important conversations. too little, too late. so if it's not about the effects of the bomb... what is this about? the title suggests the subject is the man, but i didn't even become familiar enough with him to understand him, much less identify with him. his infidelity is either easily glossed over or played for laughs. his reaction to the impending loss of his q-clearance seems a bigger loss than his bombs dropped on nagasaki & hiroshima. idk man. what are we doing here. specific nolan-isms i noticed in this film — he loves a blameless martyr of a man. a man who is as much a product of his circumstances, his era, his society as he is tortured by them. i often do this with my d&d characters, so i understand the appeal. but dude... at what point does this go beyond a preference and into an inability to deal with actual nuance? or moral grayness? i hear odysseus is given the same treatment and i personally think that's an unforgivable way to mangle him beyond recognition — everything feels so... inhuman. the interpersonal relationships are lacking—why did jean & kitty even like this guy? why is einstein reduced to the wise old wizard role?—and i even felt alienated from oppenheimer himself (see above). — loud ≠ emotionally powerful. the score itself is good, but i don't think it's very well-utilized. it's wielded like a cudgel at times and those instances of dramatic loudness just felt like heavy-handed (and wholly unsuccessful) attempts at emotional manipulation. disappointing

Revisiting Nolan #12: ‘Oppenheimer’ gets a lot of praise that I didn’t understand when I left the theatre. I was somewhat bored by this incredible interesting subject. But, I thought it was because of the most loudest experience I ever had in IMAX. So, I really hoped this rewatch would change my mind and offer a different ride. Alas, I still think this isn’t all that. While Nolan sure knows how to capture a movie on film his non-linear shenanigans kills every momentum. This structure works for some of his movies (Memento, The Prestige), but not for all. On top of that I really hated the fragmented storytelling as well. Not one scene plays, for what feels like, longer than 1 minute tops. It doesn’t enhance the viewing experience, it makes it an exhausting one. I also don’t really have the feeling that I know Oppie, or any of the other characters as well because of it. It doesn’t make me find them interesting, which doesn’t make me care about any of them, which makes me not invested in any of them. It just turns me off in so many ways. The movie is also way too long. After the 40th interrogation/hearing scene I just about had it and really thought this could’ve used a 40-45 minute trimming. I’m so sad the newer output of Nolan doesn’t appear to appeal to me anymore. I really loved his work and still can’t deny his craftsmanship as a director. Visually his movies are amazing, he gets top notch performances from his cast, his movies will stand the test of time as he goes as much practical as he can,… List goes on and on. But, I also can’t deny he’s boring the shit out of me and can’t quite hold my attention anymore. People compare this with Stone’s ‘JFK’, and I get and see that, but that movie is a million times better than this.

Unfortunately Oppenheimer was exactly as I suspected it would be: Lots of intellectual dick-swinging and acting/dialogue that is generally bland and cold as unseasoned, leftover chicken breast with not much actual artistry or depth. Nolan’s filmmaking style in general doesn’t do much for me despite my efforts to appreciate it more. It's lots of shiny spectacle and technicality with some awkward editing peppered throughout and an at times overpowering and distracting score. As per usual ( Interstellar aside) not a single character resonated with me emotionally. Even Oppenheimer himself as an antihero didn’t really reach me on a human level. What exactly was I supposed to feel here? I will say that it's far more visually compelling in regards to the cinematography and color grading than The Odyssey , and I think it also features some of Nolan's strongest casting choices (I am prepared to die on this hill). A major gripe I have though is that once again the women only exist to propel, serve and revolve around the male characters. As critic Angelica Jade Bastién has stated, “Nolan’s genius ends when a woman enters the frame.” Regardless of whether or not he’s actually misogynist I can’t help but feel as if his films generally come across that way, even if it really is unintentional. Florence Pugh (Jean Tatlock) seems to only exist as an empty and tragic sexual reprieve from all of the overwrought exposition. Emily Blunt (Kitty Oppenheimer) plays a neglected wife and mother who’s reduced to anger, tears, and alcoholism. Little empathy is shown to either, neither of them really have any agency. Also why was there not more Lilli Hornig (Olivia Thirlby)? Or Charlotte Serber (Jessica Erin Martin)? There are so many opportunities for Nolan to really expand and empower the women in his films, yet he consistently falls short. If someone goes in knowing very little or nothing at all about the subject matter then it's a decent depiction of the Manhattan Project and Oppenheimer as a person. But if you’re already well-versed in the lore--and aren’t a history buff who simply loves anything in relation to it--save yourself the time and energy by watching Kubrick's Dr. Strangelove instead. I'd personally rather watch a razor-sharp satire about the catastrophic potential of the atomic age that is as funny as it is well-acted (and it’s only 95 minutes)! Some (superficial) highlights: - Cillian Murphy being Cillian Murphy (i.e. a stone cold fox). - The casting of David "I've got a dick on my face, don't I?" Krumholtz (iykyk). - Roughly six minutes of Florence Pugh (I love her and I'll take what I can get). - Josh Hartnett giving Harrison Ford in Raiders of the Lost Ark vibes with those slutty little glasses (he's truly aged like a fine wine).

Nolan, il regista “perfetto”, non cerca la perfezione nei dettagli imperfetti alla Kubrick, cerca la perfezione nei suoi film come se fosse una formula matematica, dando a me personalmente la parvenza di una narrazione svuotata d’anima, perché per quanto possa essere toccante la storia di Oppenheimer, quanto da brividi possa essere l’interpretazione di Cillian Murphy e del resto del cast, quanto impatto visivo, scenografia ottima e quant’altro ci vuoi inserire nella lista dei pregi, questo film è la consolazione di un “distruttore”, che già moralmente è discutibile, ma sicuramente le emozioni arrivano bene e lo sa far recepire a modino, e pertanto mi trovo per tutta la durata del film a compiangere il dottor Oppenheimer con quella sensazione simile a come se fossi davanti ad una montagna, la quale dietro si celano le reali vittime dei gravissimi accaduti, Nolan lo sa, e non credo abbia avuto forti riflessioni morali sul se e il come inscenare le vicende senza trattare le vittime di Hiroshima e Nagasaki con superficialità, ma ancora una volta credo abbia avuto riflessioni “estetiche e matematiche” sul come realizzare il film perfetto Nolaniano , perché Nolan fa film analizzati teoricamente , fa film “perfetti”, emozionanti, ma che alla fine non emozionano se stesso, e neanche me perché non ci casco più. Per me sei un genio del cinema, e talvolta i geni sono incompresi, nel mondo nuovo hai avuto la fortuna di diventare il fenomeno del cinema d’oggi, ma un genio è consapevole di se e ha un ego, e il seguire completamente le proprie idee portano a perderti, e tu ti perdi in ogni film quando si tratta di trasmettere un emozione che “spacchi” lo schermo, che non sembri piatta o pensata apposta.

"When I came to you with those calculations, we thought we might start a chain reaction that would destroy the entire world." Oppenheimer is a movie with a message... but the message is far more memorable than the movie itself. Make no mistake: Christopher Nolan's film, which won seven Academy Awards including best picture and best director, is an impressive technical milestone, particularly for its score, sound design, and maybe editing. I say "maybe" editing because though Jennifer Lame has overall succeeded in condensing an encyclopedia of information into a three hour film and making it (mostly) involving, the story is extremely hard to follow. Not just sequences, but individual scenes look disjointed. There may have been a stronger sense of setup and payoff if the footage was differently arranged, and better shot (more on that later). I also wonder how much of the material we actually needed to understand the film's main point, which is that the invention of a divinely powerful weapon will destroy the world in one way or another. The first two hours of the film detail the creation and testing of the atomic bomb, while the last hour focuses on Admiral Strauss manipulating the 1954 Gray Board hearing to ruin Oppenheimer's reputation. This latter event felt extremely petty and trivial in comparison to the tragedies of World War II, but as the final scene reveals, maybe that was the point. Strauss's egotism is like a bomb that, when ignited, wrecks the dignity of those who are the unfortunate target. But I still did not care about this subplot, despite it being historically accurate (I think), and I would have been more interested in the drama between Oppenheimer and his former assistant, Edward Teller. Then there is Nolan's typical lack of camera direction; most of the dialogue scenes (which constitute maybe 90 percent of the film) simply cut back and forth between actors who dump exposition and scientific formulas in monotonous voices in front of plain-looking backgrounds. Films like Inception are similarly guilty, but Nolan's best films are often redeemed by his imaginative premises (e.g. a dream within a dream). But once Nolan began to direct stories that weren't his own, his films - at least for me - lost their flavor. It is the main criticism that I have against The Odyssey and, to a marginally lesser extent, Oppenheimer . Nevertheless, Oppenheimer forces viewers to think critically about the moral implications of using such dangerous weapons at will. Should we play with fire just because we can? It is an extremely important message in today's world, and that alone makes the film worth watching at least once. As a piece of entertainment, however, the film falters. This was my third viewing, and I still zoned out several times throughout the movie. Most people seem to love Oppenheimer , but for me, it does not "take in the sheets."

My 7-year-old son sat and watched maybe 15 minutes of this with me (it started with the sequence where they coin the word “kiloton”), and he was transfixed. I found this story to be very strong, especially because of its depth, philosophy, ideology and emotional impact. The strongest areas were: Conclusion – 5/5 Ideology – 5/5: guilt and consequences, communism Philosophy – 5/5: moral responsibility, science vs politics Quotes – 5/5: “I believe we did”, “I feel blood on my hands” Depth – 5/5: moral guilt, subjective perspectives Peaks – 5/5: The Trinity Test, the final conversation Emotion – 5/5 Symbolism – 5/5: Prometheus, the poisoned apple Main Character – 5/5 The story was particularly successful at exploring moral guilt, responsibility and the consequences of scientific discovery. The lowest score was Enjoyment – 3.5/5. Although the story was thought-provoking and well-developed, it wasn't always the most enjoyable experience but it was very interesting. Overall I would rate the story highly because of its powerful themes, philosophical ideas, symbolism and emotional moments. Its biggest strength is how it makes the reader question who is responsible for the consequences of scientific progress.

Christopher Nolan does it again in a brilliant but terrifying 3 hour film about the life of J. Robert Oppenheimer. Honestly I've been waiting to watch this for 3 years since it released. After the hype dies down usually makes the film even more of an amazing experience. At the start of this I was a bit disconnected because I forgot how loud the music is in Christopher Nolan's films. I barely could understand like the first 20 minutes of dialogue. But as everything ramped up I really got immersed in this. I don't really know that much/cared to know that much about American history despite being American lol. But this was definitely very fascinating. I always just knew Oppenheimer was the creator of the nuclear bomb. I never knew how deeply complex, flawed & very convicted he was. This gave me such a new and thoughtful insight of the history of America and the current country. This did make the nuclear bomb even more terrifying than I previously thought it was. This story was so tense & raw that it felt so alive to me. Even despite the fact its based on a true story. I was expecting all the science related stuff to be very confusing, but I surprisingly followed it very well. The cast all brought such authentic performances, I didn't at all feel like I was watching actors but instead watching characters. Cillian Murphy brought such a raw & grounded performance to Oppenheimer that I could've never imagined. Robert Downey Jr. also brought a very tense and chaotic performance to this. Besides them there are still so many great actors in this one film. Florence Pugh, Emily Blunt, Matt Damon, Benny Safdie, Gary Oldman etc. It's almost too many to count. A lot of their individual characters really deepen the psychological & emotional weight of the story. I found the story to be very moving & intellectual. Christopher Nolan is on the verge of becoming my favorite director at this rate. I haven't seen a film of his I've disliked. Interstellar & his batman films are still my personal favorites, but man this was incredible. This just now made me realize he actually writes all his films as well, which makes this film even more captivating. His visual style always flows with the story, I love how he refuses to use CGI. It makes for some very beautifully pleasant scenes. I have no idea how he managed this but its incredible. There is so many subtle but seamless visual spectacles in this. The way both the music and the directing is so atmospheric it really immersed me. Despite the music being incredibly loud it still was amazing and chilling. I think I might say this too often, but it's been a while since a film has really given me as thought provoking questions as this did. That ending was honestly very astonishing, even now it shows the weight of what Oppenheimer really created. This was both a chilling and poetic emotional exploration of humanity as a whole. Such an amazing cinematic experience.

I just find this movie so potent in a way that really sticks with me long after finishing the film. The last hour is actually quite strong! You can’t just have dudes getting together to do cool science and then not face any of the consequences of blowing up hundreds of thousands of civilians. Yes, this is depicted through a series of bureaucratic hearings but this is the way our world actually works! And it’s a miracle that these arcane procedures are shot and acted in a way that is genuinely propulsive and compelling. Look, this story—smart guys with minimal convictions working on the “scientific question of their time” in a race against the enemy—is actually compelling it happens all the time. It’s happening now! Years from now, when we’re dealing with the wreckage of what our scientific and political leaders have wrought, there will probably be backroom hearings to hash out weird grudges and judge the decision making of these leaders. And I’m sure some of the people pulling our world closer to disaster today will wring their hands over what they “had to do” while others will continue to accelerate us toward our destruction. It’s not very hopeful but you have to admit this is probably what’s going to happen.
Nolan harnesses everything he’s been doing throughout his career to produce a work beyond any expected boundaries. Enrapturing, propulsive, mind-boggling, terrifying, and absolutely masterful.

Parasite était un film que je voulais à tout prix découvrir au vu de son extrême popularité entre l'oscar du meilleur film, la palme d'or à Cannes, le film du siècle selon New York Times et j'en passe mais... Je m'attendais clairement à mieux surtout avec des thèmes comme le taux de chômage, les inégalités sociales et le côté psychologique en plus du fait que j'avais plutôt aimé Mickey 17 du même réalisateur et au final Parasite est un film qui part dans tous les sens sans vraiment développer certaines choses comme le lien entre notre personnage principal et la fille de riche dont il donne des cours d'anglais ou même la fin où le film vrille complètement sans essayer de spoiler. Heureusement que les idées étaient présentent comme le concept qui pourrait paraître simple mais qui renforce un aspect psychologique tout en dénonçant les classes sociales en Corée. La performance des acteurs est plutôt bonne en particulier pour l'actrice qui joue la professeur d'art plastique du fils des riches. En clair c'est surtout un film qui comme Anora se regarde surtout par le côté technique de l'œuvre et pas réellement par rapport à ce qu'il raconte mais je suis curieux d'une chose désormais, ça serait de le revoir mais en noir et blanc car il me semble qu'il existe une version de Parasite sous cet angle là donc cela m'intrigue fortement.

Eu amo filmes que fazem críticas sociais ou que me fazem enxergar o mundo de outra forma. Esse é um dos filmes que me fez enxergar isso. O fato de haver uma metáfora que diz ter uma linha que separa os ricos dos pobres no filme, que embora não exista uma linha física pintada no chão que separe ricos e pobres, me faz gostar muito da simbolização visual do filme. Me faz ver também a geografia da cidade: a família Kim (pobre) mora em um semiporão, abaixo do nível da rua, enquanto a família Park (rica) vive em uma casa no alto de uma colina. Sempre que os Kim voltam para casa, eles descem inúmeras escadas; quando vão à casa dos Park, sobem. A diferença de altitude simboliza a hierarquia social. Também me pegou muito a fala da mãe sobre as baratas e a cena em que eles se escondem em qualquer canto quando a família chega, fazendo uma analogia às baratas. Mas ainda assim eu acho que o filme se perdeu um pouco no final. Pra conseguir assistir a esse filme só dá se for legendado, porque dublado é terrível.

Bong Joon-ho didn't just direct a movie; he orchestrated a sleek, parasitic masterclass in late-stage capitalism that completely shatters your worldview before you even realize you're bleeding. It is a gloriously unhinged, darkly hilarious, and utterly ruthless fever dream that takes a sharp, aesthetic scalpel to class warfare and leaves you wildly entertained yet profoundly disturbed. Call Me by Your Name’s cum peach walked so Parasite’s killer peach could absolute-fuckin-run, and I need everyone to start treating Bong Joon-ho’s allergic weaponization of stone fruit with the cinematic reverence it genuinely deserves. This movie is a hyper-slick, brilliantly depraved masterclass in social divide that completely reshuffled my brain chemistry. Crazy Rich Asians walked with its pristine, gilded wealth fantasy so that the outrageously out-of-touch Park family could literally get stabbed in the backyard, proving that the absolute peak of modern cinema is watching the ultra-rich get their delicate, expensive bubble shattered by the raw, suffocating reality of the working class. The absolute chokehold this film has on me is permanent, and I swear to god I be in the club requesting "Jessica, only child, Illinois, Chicago, classmate of Kim Jin-mo, he's your cousin, ding dong" like it’s the hottest track on the charts. Park So-dam flicking that lighter on top of the overflowing toilet in the middle of a catastrophic flood is officially my eternal mood board, capturing that exact, unbothered IT-girl energy even when the world is literally drowning in sewage. It’s a breathtakingly sharp, wildly chaotic masterpiece that lures you in with scammer-family comedy only to leave you paralyzed by the tragic, impossible illusion of upward mobility. 10/10, no notes, permanently playing that door-chime jingle on loop in my mind forever.

Parasite feels so far removed from the formulaic Hollywood drivel continually thrust upon us that I’d almost forgotten films were allowed to behave like this. I loved the pacing. The patience of it. The way the camera just lingers and lets you look. Framing the entire outside world through that little ground-level basement window. People pissing outside it. Fumigation drifting through it. There’s something about making a window both your view of the world and a constant reminder of your place in it that really got me. And I loved the father. That quiet, almost performative resilience of a man the world simply will not give a fucking break. He’s funny and pathetic and dignified and increasingly broken, sometimes all at once. Actually, that might be what I love about Korean cinema in general. Everyone can feel slightly larger than life while simultaneously behaving like the sanest person in the room. Parasite can be hilarious, then sad, then horrifying, and apparently nobody told it those things are supposed to take turns. Brilliant film. And proof that, given sufficient context, even a pair of drying socks can have more screen presence than most Hollywood leads.

Je comprends totalement la hype autour de Parasite . C'est un film qui explore avec une incroyable modernité les inégalités sociales et la lutte des classes. Cette question dépasse de loin le cas de la Corée du Sud. Toute la mise en scène repose sur un véritable champ lexical visuel du parasite. Les personnages s'infiltrent, se cachent, occupent des espaces qui ne sont pas les leurs, jusqu'à devenir eux-mêmes des êtres jugés indésirables par la société. Pourtant, ils restent indispensables au fonctionnement de celle-ci. C'est une idée simple mais qui est montré comme je ne l'avais jamais vu. Le fait d'opposer deux familles est également très pertinent, car il permet de les comparer sous tous les angles. Le film est réalisé avec une telle maîtrise qu'il nous place dans une position de spectateur presque neutre. Il n'idéalise jamais la famille pauvre et ne diabolise pas non plus la famille riche. Malgré cela, les actions des personnages nous poussent naturellement à éprouver davantage d'empathie pour les plus démunis. Bien que (je me répète) ils sont loin d'être parfait. Cette satire sociale est, selon moi, bien plus aboutie que celle de Mickey 17 , pourtant réalisée par le même cinéaste. Elle est plus subtile, plus mature et laisse davantage de place à l'interprétation. Visuellement, le film est très réussi. Les jeux de lumière, notamment dans la nuit, sont magnifiques. J'aime beaucoup le contraste entre l'aspect lisse et presque irréel de la maison des riches et l'image plus texturée des rues où vit la famille Kim. On a presque l'impression que la famille Park évolue dans une publicité, coupée du monde réel. Cette idée est d'ailleurs renforcée par l'affiche du film, que je trouve excellente. Elle m'a rappelé, sans doute involontairement, celle de La Zone d'intérêt . Les deux œuvres partagent cette manière de montrer des personnages vivant dans un confort presque hermétique, au point d'ignorer ce qui se déroule juste à côté d'eux. Le parallèle est pertinent je trouve. Bref, un film incroyable. Une satire brillante, portée par des personnages d'une grande subtilité et un récit capable d'être aussi drôle que cru.

À chaque fois que quelqu'un dit qu'il aime le cinéma coréen, il ne pense qu'à deux films, "Old Boy" ou "Parasite", et c'est de ce second film dont je vais parler. De manière générale, l'histoire est très bien, les acteurs jouent parfaitement leur rôle et la tension est très dosée comme il faut. Cependant je trouve qu'il y a un côté trop "chapitres". L'histoire avance et des évènements qu'on ne peut pas du tout deviner nous tombent dessus pour changer du tout au tout le genre de l'œuvre. Le changement de ton est trop brutal à mon goût, surtout à la fin où on est à la limite de la scène bordélique. Alors oui la fin est bien et ce côté brut doit être fait exprès, mais je trouve ça désagréable. D'un autre côté le film aborde très bien le sujet des inégalités sociales et du mépris de classe qui se voit à travers des réflexions faites par la famille Clark. Pour moi ce n'est pas un chef-d'œuvre absolu, mais je peux tout de même comprendre l'engouement autour de ce film, et si ça peut donner envie aux gens de regarder autre chose que du cinéma étasunien, alors tant mieux.

Parasite was a strong and memorable film that genuinely surprised me. The story felt different from what I usually watch, yet it remained consistently interesting. The characters were very well written, making it easy to get attached to them especially the Kim family. I also really liked the film’s message and the way it was delivered. It doesn’t lecture the audience about inequality; instead, it shows how deeply class divides shape people’s lives, choices, and even their sense of dignity, often in quiet, painful, and sometimes darkly funny ways. One of the most impressive aspects was the shift into thriller territory. It never felt sudden or forced. Instead, the tension kept building gradually, and you could almost feel the emotions accumulating until they finally exploded. That careful preparation made the transition land with real impact. I connected with the entire Kim family, but the relationship that stayed with me the most was the one between Moon-gwang and her husband Geun-sae. There was something powerful in her loyalty and sacrifice that left a lasting impression. The film portrays the theme of social class with striking clarity. The contrast between the Kims’ semi-basement existence and the Parks’ spacious, sunlit house constantly reminds you how differently the same world can look depending on where you stand. The ending, especially the visualization of Ki-woo’s goal earning enough money to one day buy the house and reunite with his father felt particularly strong and emotional. My only real issue was with Ki-jung. At times she is presented as intelligent and capable, but then in certain moments (like the scene where she nervously repeats the made-up formula with her brother before the first lesson) she suddenly feels much weaker. Right after that she becomes tough and composed again. Because of these shifts, I never quite got a clear sense of who she was supposed to be, and her character ended up feeling inconsistent. Overall, a powerful and memorable film.

Perfectly executed!! "This is so metaphorical." is the perfect summary of this movie. I haven't read any analysis about the movie, but what's interesting here is that the conflict between the poor and the rich, which we ought to expect from the plot to be the main idea, isn't really the main idea. Surprisingly, the central conflict of the show is between the poor and the poor. As the rich are organized, happily in peace and harmony (shown in the party scene), the poor are fragmented and extremely bloodthirsty, drowned by their ambition to compete for scraps and leftovers, to survive by any means necessary. The song choice are very underappreciated; they carried a HUGE part of the movie. Though the ending was unsatisfying because it was unrealistic. I'll spoil a little: One hit to the head is enough to kill a man, and it would be better for the movie if it ended like that instead of making him hang around. It ruins the value of the previous scene. And the side characters were very underdeveloped, with very little conclusion. What happened to the rich family? What happened to that Min guy? What's the relationship between the son and the Min guy afterwards? It's like they built these tensions for hours just to never finish them properly.

I've returned to this movie because I got told this was the "best film ever" and since I liked the person I wanted to give it a try again. And after spending some time on my letterboxd profile to determine what my "best film ever" was (a question I was not able to answer her and still cannot, but it would probably be either be part of the post-revolutionary russian Cinema or German expressionism), I revisited parasite. Its an excellent movie. Well shot (even though it barely pushes beyond its own contructions and invent something new)  and excellently written, it inspired the emergence of a whole new sub-genre and yet I can't bend my mind around the mixed consciousness the movie expresses, embodiying my main criticism of the whole "kill-the-rich-cinema" as a whole, in that it on the one hand cannot look beyond the personifications of capitalism and cannot show a way beyond the social-democratic transcendence through the classes. Is it the best movie ever? Maybe, but it sure is pretty good.

I finally watched it guys 🥹🥹. Parasite is one of those movies that I've always wanted to watch but never got around to for whatever reason until last night (this is one of the first movies I added to my watchlist iirc) and I'm so glad that I finally did 🥹. I normally don't give something a 5 unless it's something I deeply resonate with emotionally and I don't get much out of that from Parasite if I'm being honest, but this is just such a technical marvel in every sense of the word that I can't help but give it the rating it deserves. Totally deserving of it's modern classic status and one of my new favourite movies (even if I'm not quite sure where it ranks yet). SPOILERS I'm definitely going to come back to this and give it a longer review some time in the future but for now I want to get some of my general thoughts out there. For one, this is one of the most entertaining movies of all time. Pretty much everything from that montage towards the start to the very end of the movie is filled with so many intense sequences, great dialogue, and fantastic moments that the film had me going crazy for most of the runtime. It's just such an entertaining movie front to back that I had an amazing time with. Another great aspect of this film is the symbolism but I don't have much to say in this regard as of now. It's clear that the rock for example symbolises something and I don't know what yet but things like that throughout the movie are so fascinating that I felt like I had to mention it. The main thing that makes this film stand out is it's messaging and depiction of class struggle and I found it super compelling. The way the Kim family compromises all of their morals just for financial stability shows just how much poverty can destroy your very essence as a person which is such a compelling idea. One review on here suggested that the line from Ki-Woo towards the end of the film about how his doctor and lawyer didn't look anything like a doctor or lawyer could suggest that these people are also pretending which is astounding. The capitalist society we live in forces EVERYONE to play a part just so they can live somewhat comfortably. As of now my only real complaint was how Ki-Woo getting brain damage played out. The scene of it happening and the ensuing scenes of him constantly laughing were absolutely shocking but then he's pretty much back to normal and I do think this works for the ending scene and his promise to help his father (which is a phenomenal ending btw) but I still felt that the quick change was a bit odd but that's more of a nitpick than anything. Anyways yeah definitely met, or even exceeded my expectations. Seeing this completely unspoiled was an experience I don't think I'll ever forget and I will definitely be coming back to this a lot in the future.

Por que esse filme aí tem nada a ver com o anime? Parasita é uma poesia visual e é até difícil falar o porque esse filme é tão perfeito sem dar spoiler, mas vamos lá. Vamos começar com o maestro da obra, Bong Joon-ho dirige o filme com uma maestria cirúrgica, não tem uma sequência ruim aqui, todas são extremamente a inventivas e incríveis, a direção fica o tempo inteiro brincando com o público, seja com planos mais cômicos ou tensos a primeira vista, mas que está subvertendo seus temas e até enganando o espectador. Vale dizer que o filme está CHEIO de rimas visuais, parece que cada take do filme está inserido ali de forma muito inteligente e cada composição presente conta alguma coisa. Outra obra prima desse filme é o seu enredo e seu roteiro, a trama guia e engana o espectador de maneira brilhante. O jeito que as coisas vão acontecendo é espetacular e o jeito que ele vai escalonando de uma maneira tão irreal mas ao mesmo tempo extremamente real. As atuações aqui são incríveis, todo mundo manda muito bem em seus devidos papéis, mas um em específico me chamou a atenção, Song Kang-ho transmite tudo apenas pelo olhar, ele apresenta uma atuação simplesmente maravilhosa. Tematicamente o filme é muito forte, o tema tratado aqui já é forte por si só, mas esse filme não fica na mesmisse de obras que tratam desse tema, ele vai além, ele compara, ele mostra, ele rima a situação dos personagens com situações reais, ele sai do preto e branco e nós traz algo novo e esse "novo" é genial. A cinematografia do filme é linda linda linda, tem takes maravilhosamente doloridos, mas muitos takes aqui tem uma beleza mórbida. Queria chamar atenção pra montagem do filme que faz um trabalho incrível, tudo é muito bem encaixado e torna o filme extremamente fluido. Em suma, Parasita é uma obra prima do cinema, o filme todo além de possuir um enredo e um roteiro maravilhoso, uma direção espetacular, uma temática forte e o filme tem tantas rimas visuais que o filme por si só se torna uma poesia visual.

I’m not sure this film should be classified as horror; to me it was more of a disturbing drama sprinkled with a handful of gory murders. Just as with “X”, the previous film that kicked off the trilogy of which “Pearl” is the second entry, a great deal of the film was spent building plot and the first murder occurred exactly at the one-hour mark. I don’t think anyone can deny that this film looks REALLY good. Other reviewers who note a resemblance to “The Wizard of Oz” are not to be commended on their keen perception; the director made it absolutely clear that is what he was going for. From the opening shot which mirrors Dorothy‘s arrival in Oz to the vintage title fonts and styles to the sumptuous colors throughout, one half expects a group of Munchkins to emerge from the cornfield at any time. While I felt that Jenna Ortega might have possessed greater screen presence in the first movie despite her smaller part, there is no rival to Mia Goth in this one. She owns the screen and creates a complex and (almost) sympathetic character in Pearl. It would be interesting to rewatch “X” with an eye on the older version of the character, which I did not even realize on the first viewing was played by Mia Goth. That shows you how keen my perception is. The conventional wisdom of all reviews I have seen is that “Maxxxine”, the third film in the trilogy, is the weakest of the three. But as “X” was good enough to get me to watch “Pearl”, so “Pearl” is good enough to carry me through to finish the trilogy.

Mia Goth is the goat. Her acting prowess is unreal — you can feel every ounce of her anger, and her confusion over why she just wants to kill. But I don’t get the why. Where does it come from, and how? And how did she end up with a wild crocodile as a pet? I have all these pieces I’m trying to put together to understand her. I wanted to feel it, not just hear it all explained in that long one-take monologue (still an amazing performance, though). It’s eerie. Her stance, her stares, that’s everything this film is. That’s what creates all the horror. But the whys and hows still left me with way too many questions.

www.fastretailing.com/eng/about/company/profile_yanai-koji.html so the film gives some nod to the fact that there's discontent within this worker despite his happy veneer throughout everything else that had transpired until that point. but does it explain what this could be or how it could come to happen? there is some interpersonal drama and we witness some cheating, but there is little if any attention paid to the structure these things exist in. when his coworker disappears and a new person shows up the next day, this just happens. the higher ups have taken care of it. and no further questions are asked. in [this one interview] yakusho says that his character sees the homeless man in the intersection and is moved by that he's the only one to really do so; but does he? this is a caricature too! and the film dupes us because we're grafted onto him. we have no choice in the operation, and it's made sure of that every step of the way. the whole thing is choreographed form the very beginning. take the tic-tac-to game, for example; there you have yakusho initially thinking it's just trash. the audience at this point is like, no! what are you doing, don't you see there's greater value there!! but then he realizes his mistake and even plays along. and this becomes a subplot of the film, of him filling out the tic-tac-to game, playing against some yet unseen opponent. and then when the game is over, he gets a thank you note for his role as such. and we get satisfaction in this because he did what we wanted him to. the film shines light on his face when his coworker's (ex?)girlfriend suddenly kisses him, but don't worry, it's just the light of the car door suddenly opening, no secondary function here. (by which i mean to say that this is specifically queuing us to receive this scene in a certain way). we get led along the whole time and then at the end there this pretense that it was all worth it but that life's tough and you just have to keep on. but what the real final shot is, it need be understood, gives the actual game away. that is, the grand city scape and the shining sun. while i'm not anti-city or anything like this, it's necessary to understand the relation to city that this film has from the point of its very inception. this is literally a propaganda piece for The Tokyo Toilet initiative -- an "urban revitalization" (we can just say gentrification, you don't have to be so coy) program masterminded by Yanai Koji, son of Uniqlo's CEO Yanai Tadashi. we can get another glimpse of this in a chance scene that happens when Yakusho comes across an older man standing in front of a developing plot. The old man asks Yakusho if he remembers what used to be here. Yakusho doesn't answer and the old man concludes, that's what it means to get old (you forget what used to be). But this is literally not true! Or, it doesn't have to be. It is not an inevitability of life that high end toilets financed by plastic industry and fast fashion will displace the perfectly functioning ones that existed before. It's not the fault of the people for forgetting, it's that there's a literal ongoing violence that makes people forget. And then part of this too can be the whole system of atomization that this is all tied up in, where people just exist as individual subjects, maybe tending to their own idiosyncratic archive, but there is no collective knowledge share -- there is no means of coming together and producing a history of what things have been like so that this knowledge can be passed down to future generations. Instead you get family heirlooms and hand-me-downs. Everything is purely familial, the film wants us to believe. Which has problems because generational wealth doesn't exist! This shit is stolen goods. And then so what, it's just too bad for people that never got a foothold to begin with? There has to be a better way. (More to come; this as to be the start of a research project; permitting everything goes alright tonight).

El monótono y rutinario trabajo de un limpiador de baños en Tokio, con una vida aburrida y rutinaria en un entorno aburrido y rutinario día tras día hasta la llegada de una visita Sigo sorprendido unos días después de como una historia absolutamente ABURRIDA tiene comentarios que la consideran algo notable en el cine de los últimos años. Dos horas de la vida de un señor que limpia baños públicos en Tokio, amanece, trabaja, baño, come, lee y vuelta a empezar salvo un trozo tras HORA Y CUARTO DE LO MISMO donde aparece la sobrina y medio entiendes algo de todo esto. Sinceramente y con todo el respeto me gustaría saber a qué se debe tanto halago a una película donde su guion no es nada, solo destaca la actuación del protagonista y tirar de éxitos musicales de los 70. ¿Qué nos quiere decir Wenders? Debes ser feliz desde una vida rutinaria y monótona, sino pues te jodes. Cinematográficamente la película tiene un par de cositas buenas: -	Protagonista despierta simpatía + ambigüedad en su pasado. -	La fotografía está elaborada y cuidada. El mensaje se podría haber resumido en 15 minutos, como mucho podría ser un corto. Parece una coña pero la película surge cuando el Tokio Toilet Project invitó a Wim Wenders a la capital para que observara los aseos públicos que habían diseñado famosos arquitectos en Shibuya. Wenders está prendado de Japón y su mundo desde hace décadas e interesado en la arquitectura del país. La idea era que creara cuatro cortos documentales sobre esos baños públicos, acabamos teniendo esto. Lo mejor: Tirar de clásicos de la música. Lo peor: Su pompa de otra película que ha inventado el cine.

Dear Wim Wenders, I've tried, man. I really tried with this one. Your films, while esthetically pleasing, carry nothing in terms of substance, story, or attention. I'm not saying I need action packed, narrative expository, tiktok noise to keep me invested, but Jesus Christ, Wim, give me something to work with. Your films are flat. They engage with the lonely side of life and less about the slice of it - and that's something to be commended for. But not everyone is lonely. Not everyone feels that way. And sometimes a lonely day is not that engaging. If I wanted to see a lonely slice of life piece that's a little more engaging, I would rather just watch a documentary. I'm sorry Wim, but I feel you will never write anything that's neither engaging or worth my time. The closest you got to making a film that explores loneliness while keeping your audience somewhat entertained was 42 years ago and it definitely shows. Maybe you're a lonely man who wants everyone else to feel as lonely as you, and maybe that's the point of your films. But I don't to feel that way everytime I want to engage with your art. You'll never change and that's okay, but I don't think I'll invest in your talent ever again. Your fans are few but dedicated, and your quality speaks to them in ways that I will never comprehend. I'm sorry I can never be part of that dedicated community that sees the beauty of your world, and I'm sorry I can't see what you see. Maybe someday I might, but not banking on that anymore. But keep making your art anyway. Film as a whole needs voices like yours. Sincerely, A.F.X. Heller

C’est un désastre politique on le sait, le riche dans la cinquantaine qui fui vers le bas en nettoyant les toilettes et qui le fait avec joie en contemplant les petits moments tout le monde en a assez parler. J’aime bien l’idée quand même, car d’une certaine manière, sans le faire exprès, wenders montre un truc auquel il a peut être pas pensé. C’est parce que le protagoniste est transfuge, parce qu’il a un certain capital culturel, une certaine sensibilité à la vie bonne qu’il fait autant d’effort pour être heureux (parce que c’est un effort de trouver entre les moment de travaux de beaux moment) c’est parce qu’il subit pas la précarité qu’il peut se permettre ce retrait. Mais. Ça reste désastreux et encore plus qu’on pourrait imaginer : le projet vient de Koji Yanai, dirigeant de Fast Retailing (Uniqlo), qui cherchait à faire connaître ces toilettes à l’international et voulait un documentaire signé par un grand réalisateur, c’est une commande de communication autour d’un projet d’architecture financé par une multinationale du textile, transformée en méditation sur la dignité. D’où le fait principal qui choque : Oui il est heureux et digne, les toilettes sont propres, peu fréquentée etc, parce que  ce sont des objets de design signés Ando, Ban, Kuma, qui sont l’objet « pub » du film. Le film ne peut pas montrer la réalité d’un métier ingrat et dégradant, et c’est pas son but car il faut d’abord montré une société de toilettes fonctionnelles belle et propre. Ça reste une petite méditation sur l’attention au détail et aux formes de vie donc oui c’est agréable à regarder, mais on peut pas fermer les yeux sur cette botte en cuir bourgeoise mise sur la tête de tout ceux qui peuvent pas se permettre de vivre car le travail leur prend toute l’énergie qu’il faut pour avoir ne serait-ce qu’un dixième de béatitude que ressent ce gentil monsieur agent d’entretien. Bob l’éponge est littéralement plus subtile sur la question et ça se défendra en long en large et en travers le jour où j’aurais un blog.

Chato, mas necessário. O filme apesar de longo e muitas vezes entediante pra alguns, ensina que devemos sempre procurar as coisas belas mesmo que nas coisas mais simples. Ele ensina que a paz que almejamos é uma escolha que fazemos todos os dias. Sem dúvidas, a maior lição que o filme passa, é encontrar beleza e dignidade no comum, sem se importar com as cicatrizes do passado.

Demorei quase uma semana pra começar a escrever sobre esse filme, isso porque as sensações eram bem mistas e ele realmente me fez refletir sobre diversos temas. Eu gosto de como o filme começa, gosto de como a rotina ritualística de Hirayama é, apesar de repetitiva, diferente todos os dias por meio do que é ignorado, gosto da cadência com que ele nos é apresentado: aos poucos, enquanto nós só observamos sem compromisso, acompanhando a vida do protagonista sem de fato saber quem ele é. Entendo a posição contemplativa que Wenders tenta nos colocar, a de olhar através dos olhos do protagonista ou da lente de sua câmera. Creio que esse seja o principal ponto onde o longa pode ou não funcionar, a depender da capacidade individual de um espectador de enxergar beleza nessas pequenas coisas (o que não é nem um pouco fácil) e é também onde, pelo menos pra mim, Wenders fracassa em transmitir esse valor, chegando a soar artificial em certos momentos, pois o filme no fim das contas ainda é uma encomenda publicitária, e porque extrai sua beleza do que já é belo, não do que é banal e visto como tal. Não acho que o filme seja fetichista ou romantize um trabalho como o de limpador de banheiros, tampouco ingênuo em afirmar que tudo são flores e que problemas não existem, eles existem. Acredito que a escolha de não mostrar o impacto do preconceito ou do cansaço no protagonista pode ser interpretada como parte justamente da filosofia dele, e a forma como ele vive, mas até que ponto? A partir da segunda metade do filme, o usso e abuso da principal característica e filosofia de vida do personagem (resiliência estoica, contemplação, serenidade e deslocamento/distância) como justificativa para a falta de dramatização e proximidade expulsa a trama dos próprios trilhos. Parece que o filme frequentemente nos carrega pra uma situação dramática com grande peso para ele, mas sempre que algo precisa de tempo para ser sentido, até mesmo tempo para que haja a dúvida de por que um limpador de banheiros escolheria deliberadamente a vida que tem, o filme foge e inicia um novo dia, com a mesma desculpa. Tenho fé que deve existir alguém que nem o Hirayama por aí, mas que esse alguém É ou em algum momento foi/será maluco, eu tenho é certeza.

I get what Perfect Days is trying to say; the beauty of presence, routine, simplicity and finding meaning in ordinary moments. If that were my life, I honestly don’t think I’d want to keep living. The silence in this movie was so loud because he’s just... alone. I know that’s part of the point, but it made me feel isolated rather than comforted. There was also so little dialogue that for me, the pacing started to feel boring. It’s a well made film with a clear vision, but it just wasn’t for me.

I thought he’d maybe talk to the bookstore lady? Or talk to mama? Or call his niece at the end to see how she was doing? I just can’t help but see a man living in his own head, refusing to truly cherish everything life has to offer. I also loved the black and white dream sequences.

I solemnly swear that I am not being a contrarian by rating this low. On a technical level, this is not a bad film by any means. The cinematography is gorgeous, with very nice shot composition. I admired the crisp, tactile sound design. I liked the editing and thought the performances were solid. Everything else just didn’t do it for me, and I don’t think I’d recommend watching this film to anyone. I don’t wish to yuck anyone’s yum, but the level of praise this gets from people baffles me. A previous version of me would deride those people, but I now know better not to stoop to that. At the very least, I get why others appreciate it so much, I just can’t see the appeal in a way where I’m in the appreciator crowd, if that makes sense. Barely anything happens in this movie. You watch the protagonist go through the same loop: his work schedule, his hobbies, his habits, etc. There are minor deviations along the way that shake things up, but nothing intensely interesting, nor anything that really moves a strong narrative forward, with the exception of his niece showing up later in the film. Before you tell me I “missed the point”, I know for certain that I recognized the point of the film, I suppose I just don’t accept it. Maybe I don’t necessarily reject the point outright, I just don’t like the execution. It's two hours long, for the general message of appreciating life. For me, that’d be fine for a short film, but two hours just for that?! Watch a video about the importance of being present, then meditate for five minutes. You’ll get more value that way. “But, PolynesianSpa,” you say. “That’s the point. The fact that you cannot bear a two hour film about living in the moment shows that you are impatient and restless. You missed the point, for you do not appreciate the little things, you do not relish simplicity, nor do you revel in mundanity. You are incongruent with the essence of the film.” you lecture. Touché. I don’t jive with this movie on a personal level, that’s just not who I am. Still, usually I can enjoy things that I don’t directly relate to, if I like the execution enough. This just felt like a massive waste of time. Perhaps it was a lesson. I’ll admit it. I’m envious of the film’s protagonist. Hirayama lives a life of mediocrity, but that doesn’t seem to bother him. As a toilet cleaner, he is technically a vital part of the upkeep of civilization, yet I imagine it is a thankless job that does not pay as much as it should. Regardless, he does not stew in dissatisfaction. He makes the absolute most of what he has. Not me. I’ve been stuck in a slightly-above-minimum-wage job for too long. What exasperates my frustration with the film is that I myself don’t have even the slightest amount of dedication that Hirayama has. He has this unrelenting commitment to routine and work, despite said routine and work not really yielding much fulfillment. I am also of the belief, especially in our age of hypercapitalist exploitation, that one shouldn’t bust their ass for a boss/company that doesn’t care for them at all. Do your job and do it right, but don’t wear yourself out for the sake of the corporate fat cats who own you. Hirayama lacks revulsion for his overlords, choosing instead to focus on his duty. He’s achieved Nietzsche’s amor fati, a concept that I can’t fathom acquiescing to. He is complacent to his situation. I have become mostly complacent in my current status in life. I’ve avoided getting my driver’s license for about five years, and my job that I hate was only supposed to be for a gap year after high school — I am currently in my fourth year. Complacency is like a gift or skill to Hirayama, whilst it is a curse for me that I struggle to free myself from. Lying down and accepting my current state means not improving. Hirayama has mastered his lot in life, taking the routine by the reins. He has his routine down to a science, and has several locations where those who occupy them know him and have an established connection with him. I have close friends, sure, but not really any third spaces that I have integrated into my schedule. My life doesn’t operate like clockwork as Hirayama’s seems to. Granted, I’m not all bad. Sure, I struggle with productivity (took me FOREVER to write this review), but when it comes to being present and practicing gratitude, I am much better off than I once was. Coming out of an awful headspace in both my tween and teen years, in addition to a borderline mystical experience whilst on edibles, I’ve developed a stronger appreciation for life. I’m also going to school this fall, and am lined up to finally earn my license. I haven’t completely ditched my smartphone, but I bought a flip phone to keep as my main source of communication. My so-called "job that I hate" certainly could be worse. Still, a life like Hirayama’s is one I would not want to live. It looks peaceful, and he’s definitely much less neurotic than I am, but I’ve gained a sense of disgust for menial work. I want to do something meaningful and fulfilling. I tire of consuming slop and being bogged down by my stressful yet tedious job. I want to live well and make cool shit. All in due time, I guess. In the grand scheme of things, Perfect Days’ protagonist is like a background character. Disregarding the philosophical concept that we’re all finite meaningless blobs of flesh (tried to say that less pretentiously than the “floating rock” r/iam14andthisisdeep type shit), Hirayama especially is of little overall importance. He’ll likely leave no legacy, his contribution to society is not nonexistent but also isn’t monumental, and his life does not affect the lives of many others. He is quite inconsequential. He reminded me of my manager, who has told me on multiple occasions that his baseline goal in life is to live as a “background character”. Just be here, do what he can, and die a content man. I think that’s an admirable mindset to have, but the YOLO part of me finds it to be unrewarding. I don’t claim to practice what I preach, as I’m aware I’m often in a rut of passionless inaction, but I like to think my refusal to be totally complacent means that I have hope. There’s something here, I know it. The komorebi, the appreciation for music, the value of human connection, the attention to detail, the maintenance of plant life, and the ethereal quality of dreams. There are several moments that capture the indescribable lustre of life, along with the overwhelming experience of existence that makes you laugh and cry, much like Hirayama. I just found that all of that beauty was lost in the slog of seeing roughly the same thing over and over again with a few unexciting events in between. I was honestly begging for it to end at some point. Watching Perfect Days felt like watching someone else play Tomodachi Life . There’s a few brief glimmers of fun, but a majority of the time all that there is to see is a handful of characters idling around. I liked the scenes that featured 60s-70s music, it reminded me of car rides with my grandpa. The Japanese performance of “House of the Rising Sun” was very captivating. The tic-tac-toe game made me smile. My favourite scene was the shadow tag part, it was so sweet. Unfortunately, a few nuggets of brilliance scattered across a void of plotless dullness do not make an enjoyable film. This review ended up being more of a personal vent than a thorough overview of Perfect Days , but the movie felt so bland that I genuinely didn’t have much more to talk about. I didn’t care for this film on the first go ‘round, but would like to later. Perhaps next time, but not now.

No es para todos y pienso que dentro de esta especie de subgénero de películas "no pasa nada" hay mejores, pero aún así Perfect Days es una película bellísima que cambia tu forma de ver la cotidianidad de la vida, es una historia realmente sencilla, sin grandes giros ni pretenciones solo la vida de un hombre que limpia baños. Una película muy necesaria, muy contraria a lo que lo acelerado de la vida actual nos tiene acostumbrados. Me gusto mucho lo relajante que es ver está película, si bien no es la película más estímulante en cuanto a trama de la historia pues es que eso no es lo que busca daré está obra, entre la excelente dirección, la fotografía que hace que cada momento del film sea bello e incluso el sonido ambiental te transmiten muchísimo esa paz de Hirayama, de apreciar los pequeños detalles. Eso mismo los detalles son un gran acierto de Perfect Days, ver está obra por encima es un gran error, por más que sea una película en la que no pase mucho el verla de fondo es no entender lo que te está tratando de decir, cosas pequeñas como la nota del gato (#) que Hirayama dejaba en el baño, sus fotos, en indígente que siempre veía son las cosas pequeñas y fugaces que hacen en conjunto a Perfect Days una película tan especial sobre ver el mundo sin toda la prisa con lo que lo solemos ver. Un tema que me gustó como fue plasmado fueron lo choque generaciónales entre Hirayama con su sobrina y el wey que lo ayudaba a limpiar, un contraste entre la forma calmada y serena de vivir de alguien que alguien con su experiencia formó contra la forma apresurada y caótica que la juventud y la sociedad actúal tenemos. También me gustaron estás escenas intermedias surrealistas y en blanco y negro entre cada día que la película tiene, como si fueran solo instante de los recuerdos que las rutinas largas nos dan. En fin, este tipo de películas que usan un ritmo lento para resaltar los momentos pequeños siempre son las que más terminan renonando conmigo con el pasar del tiempo y Perfect Days siento que va a ser una de las que más me voy a quedar.

On this rewatch, I find this to be much more somber. The last time I saw this, I didn’t get the implication that Hirayama was physically abused as a child. I got that he withdrew from his family and seemingly a fortune because of his father. I think I read it as his father put too much pressure on him to achieve more in life. The inclusion of Patricia Highsmith’s The Terrapin seems to suggest something darker and more tragic. It certainly colors Hirayama’s interaction with his niece and sister differently. Initially, I viewed Hirayama’s solitary, humble life as his choice. Possibly, an act of rebellion. But I see it differently now. His fixation on shadow and light feels connected to this unnamed trauma he carries. And the music, his routine, and the small connections he makes are little ways he allows light to seep into his life.

15-20 minutes into the film... what a heartwarming depiction of the joy found in the everyday moments of life. 20-40 minutes into the film... okay what the fuck is wrong with this guy? ~1 hour into the film... one of the most emotionally devastating scenes I can ever remember. Such is Perfect Days, which felt wholly unlike anything I've seen before. Watching this felt like dropping a pebble in a pond or holding a mirror up to a mirror, creating a nesting reflection that stretched to space. Can it be taken at face value? A one-sentence mission statement about the beauty all around us? Or Is there some kind of dark riptide that undermines that beauty? The unspeakable rift that separates a family or the confrontation with mortality; the black and white negatives of the otherwise sun-dappled trees? Or does the contrast of those fissures again underline all the light and goodness we wake up to every morning? Perfect Days is a meditation. Or, maybe It's a haiku - its simplicity and bareness allowing the audience to graft their own meaning upon it. If one test of a writer is to see how much they can communicate with few words, then what Koji Yakusho is doing as an actor in a near silent-film performance is unbelievable. While it must have been difficult to convince studios to greenlight a movie about a janitor in which nothing happens, it's not difficult to latch on to what made this film so moving. Watching it, I felt the same way I do whenever I travel. That when I step away from the interiority of my own life and consider it from a distance I feel as if I am swept up into a greater world around me where anything is possible.

Perfect Days is only my second Wim Wenders film after Paris, Texas , and somehow he’s already given me two incredible films. I honestly feel like I may have peaked way too early with his filmography, because I don’t know how he tops either of these for me. There’s just something so beautiful about the simplicity of this film. Hirayama’s life is incredibly routine and on the surface there isn’t a huge amount happening, but Wenders makes that routine feel meaningful without ever forcing it to be. The pacing is absolutely brilliant. The film is more than happy to sit with Hirayama as he goes about his day, and I never felt bored or impatient. If anything, I found myself becoming more immersed in the rhythm of his life. The sparse dialogue works perfectly with this too. So much of Hirayama’s character is communicated through his expressions, his routines, the people he interacts with, the books he reads and especially the music he listens to. There’s very little need for exposition because the film trusts you to simply observe him and gradually piece together who he is. I also loved the visual style. The colour palette is gorgeous, the editing is really neat, and the Tokyo cityscapes are beautiful throughout. There’s something about the contrast between the busy, overwhelming city and Hirayama’s incredibly simple existence within it that I really loved. Wenders somehow makes cleaning public toilets, eating lunch in a park and driving around Tokyo listening to music feel almost meditative. It’s also interesting comparing this to Paris, Texas. They’re very different films, but there’s definitely a similar fascination with loneliness, human connection and people who have seemingly withdrawn from a previous life. Paris, Texas is much more emotionally heavy and dramatic, whereas Perfect Days feels far more content with simply observing life. It almost feels like Wenders has arrived at a more peaceful understanding of some of the same ideas. And Koji Yakusho is incredible. He does so much with so little dialogue, and the final sequence in particular is such a beautiful example of that. His face says more than pages of dialogue ever could. I think what I loved most is that Perfect Days never feels like it’s trying to convince you that Hirayama’s life is perfect. It’s just showing you that there can be something beautiful in an ordinary life if you actually pay attention to it. The repetition, the routine, the little moments of connection, the music, the trees, the photographs - all of these tiny things gradually become meaningful. This is easily the best thing I’ve seen from Wenders so far, although I’ve only seen two films, so maybe I’ve just started with an unfairly strong pair. Either way, absolutely beautiful from start to finish. 10/10 Top100

Another one for psych class. This is one of the worst films I've ever seen. The performances are mediocre, with DiCaprio's likely being the worst. The writing is incredibly juvenile, even with the plausible theory that the majority of the dialogue is filtered through the guy's warped mind. The film doesn't even look good or have an interesting aesthetic. The twist falls apart because it requires you to empathize with DiCaprio's character in the beginning, which I did not. Now, to the big problems. This film's portrayal of the mentally ill is disgusting. I understand that the facility is specifically meant to house people who've committed a violent crime, but the film was arguably still irresponsible in its perpetuation of the stereotype that all people with mental illness are scary, violent, completely irrational, and are deserving of no empathy whatsoever. There is no mention of the specific diagnosis that any patient, let alone the main character, has, which makes it impossible to understand the accuracy of the portrayals. This film was made too recently to still exhibit such an under-researched and outdated parody of what a real group of underprivileged people is like. Let's move on to another problem, the film's portrayal of both the Holocaust and the implications of Project MKUltra during the Cold War. These were both serious tragedies that I feel were not handled with appropriate sensitivity and were rather just half-baked elements seemingly thrown in for added novelty. With this film exhibiting these two themes in addition to its portrayal of extreme psychosis, there are too many things being explored and none of them are done properly. The main conspiracy is clearly supposed to be MKUltra, something that really did victimize psychiatric patients during the Cold War, and yet in the movie's cannon, it's confirmed to not be happening. I don't think this film is intentionally trying to say that MKUltra didn't happen, but it's a very strange and poorly thought-out choice that is completely at odds with the setting. This movie clearly did not have anything to say about any of the incredibly serious topics it includes, and thus has no comprehensive or unique thesis. It's an offensive, confused mess that frankly has no merit as a piece of art.

Enjoyed this more on rewatch, I was better able to appreciate how the mood of the island is developed, with the soundscape being particularly impressive, with original score, licensed music, and classical music all coming together really well. Weather is also used particularly effectively to make the island feel isolating and uncomfortable; there's something about heavy rain at night that makes me really uncomfortable and I love the way that is used in this film. The star segment here is Ward C, feeling like walking into a nightmare within an already dreadful environment - it feels like those segments in Silent Hill when you go from normal world to Otherworld, everything just gets so suddenly worse and terrifying with no end in sight. Despite this being a psychological thriller with heavy emphasis on its ending, it still does very little for me compared to the build up on the island (which I really enjoyed) and other films in the ending-heavy "genre" (Memento, Prestige, Fight Club, Total Recall, etc.). It just never feels like the reveals that happen meaningfully impact or re-contextualize the earlier scenes of the film. Of course the context does literally change but it doesn't really change the emotional impacts, at least for me

Shutter Island is a psychological thriller film directed by Martin Scorsese and released in 2010. The movie stars Leonardo DiCaprio as Teddy Daniels, a U.S. Marshal who travels to a mysterious island with his partner, Chuck Aule, to investigate the disappearance of a patient from a psychiatric hospital. As Teddy investigates, strange events begin to happen, and he starts to question the hospital, the doctors, and even his own memories. The story becomes more mysterious and confusing as Teddy discovers that the island is hiding a dark secret. One of the best things about Shutter Island is its atmosphere. The dark setting, suspenseful music, and confusing events create a feeling of fear and mystery. Leonardo DiCaprio also gives a very strong performance as Teddy. The ending is one of the most surprising parts of the movie because it changes the way we understand the whole story. Overall, Shutter Island is an interesting and suspenseful movie that makes the audience think about reality, memory, and guilt. I would recommend it to people who enjoy psychological mystery films.
