Au moins aussi acclamé à sa sortie, ce second opus a le mérite d'être divertissant, mais à l'inverse du premier qui était une montée en puissance sur tous les plans, plus les enjeux multiversels prennent du poids, et moins il convainc. Spider-Man : Across the Spider-Verse est bien meilleur lorsqu'il se concentre sur l'intime, même s'il demeure à ce sujet très classique. D'ailleurs, j'ai bien cru que je le préférerais à en juger par son introduction, plus aboutie que celle du précédent, mais la suite m'a déçu. Il est très frustrant de regarder une œuvre qui s'étend sur autant de temps pour ne pas avoir le droit à une vraie fin, fut-elle ouverte. Sur le plan visuel, on est dans la continuité, avec un peu plus de variété issue de l'exploration du multivers. Toutefois, je regrette l'inclusion de live action qui me sort totalement du film. Ponctuellement, certains plans continuent de me gêner par leur façon de trancher avec d'autres mais je dois dire que cela a moins été le cas qu'auparavant. C'est peut-être une question d'habitude, mais je pense surtout que celui-ci est techniquement plus abouti. Quoi que je sois critique, cela reste à des années lumières des bouses super-heroïques que nous sert Marvel à son habitude. Le moment est plaisant mais hormis toute la séquence où Gwen et Miles se retrouvent puis papotent en se collant sur les bâtiments — qui est superbe — je ne sais pas si j'en retiendrais grand chose sur le long terme. En fait, je me rends bien compte que toutes mes scènes préférées sont dans le premier acte. Après, comme c'est une expérience formelle, je suppose qu'il a l'avantage de bien se revoir. La sortie de la suite sera l'occassion de le réévaluer.

50 Across the Spider-Verse is a film that promises everything and delivers... some of it. The multiverse concept, inherently thrilling on paper, remains the franchise's greatest asset. The sheer variety of Spider-People is a joy to behold. The film does not disappoint in its ambition. Yet for all its formal brilliance, Across the Spider-Verse stumbles badly in its handling of tone, and nowhere is this more evident than in its villain. His early appearances are played purely for laughs, and while the film eventually attempts to pivot toward genuine menace, the damage is already done. He becomes a symbol of the film's broader comedic excess: the relentless quipping and meta-references that undercut every moment of tension. By the time The Spot transforms into a world-ending threat, we cannot take him seriously because the film never taught us how. The film's incessant needle drops compound the problem, each licensed track feeling less like organic storytelling and more like a calculated monetization strategy. The soundtrack is curated not to serve the narrative but to populate Spotify playlists, a transparent effort to generate revenue streams beyond the box office. This commercial calculation extends beyond the music. The cliffhanger ending? It is difficult not to view it as a deliberate fragmentation, a way to stretch a single story across multiple releases and maximize returns. Enjoyable as Spider-Man eye candy. It's amazing we get a Spider-Man movie where Miguel O'Hara plays such a huge role, me in the nineties never would've believed such a thing would ever happen. I enjoyed the first one well enough, it has the edge of being a self-contained movie, but O'Hara being in this one gives it a big boost. Spider-Man is a humorous, self-deprecating character, but after so many incarnations of Woody Allen in a lucha mask, getting a masculine presence like O'Hara is a welcome change. Of course, such a character can't be a good guy in a movie today, so he's presented as a villain. But he also happens to be right. Multiverses are a cheat and always suck. Even if the story does something clever with it, it's always just a device for lazy writers to worm their way out of the corners they paint themselves into. This movie explains a lot of rules for its multiverse to you, through Miguel O'Hara, who enforces said rules, only for the movie to tell you the rules don't matter and you can do whatever you want (a theme in society today, especially during the years when this film was being made). Ok pal, then I don't care about your plot. The way I stayed invested was hoping their supposed villain, the correct and true alpha chad O'Hara, gets to eventually execute the arrogant, insufferable main characters. It's not a movie with an actual ending, so I can hope it happened offscreen after the credits roll, at least until the next movie where nothing matters comes out.

I do not envy anyone given the task of following Into the Spider-Verse. That film singularly injected so much new life and artistic innovation into an IP that was beginning to get stagnant. It took the time and consideration to acknowledge the foundation and rich history baked into the character of Spider-Man and gave it a loving sendoff before turning to a brand new chapter. Regrettably, Across the Spider-Verse feels like one step forward, two steps back. If there’s one thing my journey through the MCU has taught me, it’s that the multiverse fucking sucks. And I understand that’s a contentious position to hold against a series called “the Spider-Verse,” but hear me out. Into the Spider-Verse used the concept in the most effective way: minimalistic. The multiverse purely acted as the inciting incident for Miles’ story, much like time travel in the first Terminator movie. Yes, you had cheeky references to established Spider-Man iterations, their tropes and standing in pop culture, but ultimately it was a measuring stick to hold up to Miles’ own hero’s journey. A narrative device showing how the character inspired this new hero, much like he has countless others in our own world. Comparatively, Across the Spider-Verse becomes overindulgent, languishing in its multiverse setting and using it as an excuse to showcase the less popular Spider-Man content, or ride the coattails of the more popular content. Remember Andrew Garfield Spider-Man? Look, there he is! And Toby McGuire! Look, this multiversal Spider-Man agency knows about what Dr. Strange was doing! And the dimension-hopping films? He talks to Mrs. Chen, from our hit Venom film series! The SPUM-C is alive and well. And look, there’s Donald Glover as Prowler! Like he was gonna be in the MCU! There’s also an attempt to make each dimension extremely unique, which unfortunately comes across like a more obnoxious attempt to copy the uniqueness of Into the Spider-Verse’s art style, and the clashing artstyles tend to make it look like a big, muddled mess. Really, with a concept like the multiverse, the last thing you want to do is get technical. Where Deadpool & Wolverine had the braindead concept of an anchor being, Across the Spider-Verse presents the “canon events.” (Which felt like such a dumb attempt at meta, I threw up in my mouth a little bit.) Rather than the shared trauma being a bonding point between the different iterations of Spider-Man, it’s now an absolute event necessary for their journey, whose disruption could lead to the disintegration of their reality. Delving more into the multiverse also takes the wind out of the sails for Miles’ own character arc. Spoilers: we find out that he wasn’t meant to become Spider-Man, as the spider that bit him came from another dimension. So he is an anomaly, and his arc is that, even though it wasn’t his destiny…he is still Spider-Man. Because he chooses to be. Which isn’t nothing , but feels like a much more hollow echo of his arc in the first film. My own cynicism and hangups notwithstanding, Across the Spider-Verse is a fine film. A far fall from its predecessor, but if you’ve been missing the characters and world, it does feel like a welcome return. It’s overbloated, and its standing as a definitive “part one” further lessens its value on its own, but it’s ultimately competent enough.

I wasn’t impressed when I saw this in theaters 3 years ago. I decided to give these movies a rewatch, to see if my opinion has changed. And I did like the first one more than I thought I did. As for this one? Unfortunately, still not very impressed. The weakest part of the first movie was the entire multiverse plot line. That idea has been taken and beaten to death over the years. In 2018, it was still relatively new. 2023 and now? I’ve lost all interest at this point. And this film took the multiverse concept and pushed it to the max. It did all the things that I’m already tired of. Relentless cameos and jumping across different universes at will. It’s a shame that such an original looking movie falls short in the original plot or concept department. And I’m a little iffy on the villain situation for this one. With the first, Kingpin was great because he wasn’t one note. He actually had a solid motivation for what he was trying to do. In this, it seems like Spot is the main villain, but really it’s Miguel. It’s mind boggling to me how any of the Spidermen could follow Miguel when he’s so clearly wrong. And even if he’s doing these things for the right reason, he’s a total dick about it. That’s another thing, if all these Spidermen are gathered in the same place trying to stop anomalies, who the hell is saving people in their own universes? It doesn’t make a whole lot of sense and just makes it all seem too gimmicky. This movie also lacks some of the charm that the first one had. It’s very dark and depressing, in comparison to the first which was fun and exciting. And the animation doesn’t seem as refined. I know that some of the different universes have different designs, but it’s an overall drop off from the first in quality. Now, it’s not all bad. I still enjoy the creativity and visuals overall. It’s not as good as the previous, but still better than most animated films visually. The story is also better than the first. It’s more complex and ambitious, despite being entwined in multiverse slop. And the voice acting is still top notch. But this film is also quite long. Especially when considering that it’s only half of a story. I feel like anything over 2 hours is just a little too long for any animated film. Even the higher quality ones like this series. Well, at least now I know. I do actually like the first Spiderverse movie, and this one isn’t bad, it’s just not as good as the first. It relies a little too much on the multiverse tropes while also losing some of the first’s luster. Final Verdict: 6.5/10

Я, лично, ничего тут не нашёл из «лучшей истории о Человеке-пауке», но она очень хорошая. Конечно, как гику такой фильм прикольно посмотреть, но явно не по мне. Да, тут много отсылок на пауков, много гик-намёков. По визуалу скажу: ЭТО САМЫЙ разнообразный СДВГ-контент вообще за всю Марвел. Первые 30 минут смотреть просто невозможно. ЭТОТ ФИЛЬМ ПРОСТО ОСТАНОВИТЬСЯ НЕ МОЖЕТ В ПОСТОЯННОЙ СМЕНЕ КАДРОВ И РИСОВКИ. Вырвиглазно порой было смотреть начало, но потом втягиваешься и фильм становится действительно хорошей личной историей Майлза Моралеса. Неплохо получается совмещать фильм-аттракцион, цветастое месиво для подростков, СДВГ-контент и неплохой сюжет о спасении и сохранении человечности. По сюжету в целом неплохо. Драматургия отличная и зашкаливает. Интересно, что всё таки фильм намного лучше развивает историю Мультивселенной, чем сами Marvel Studios. У Майлза, которому вообще 15 лет, начинаются самые тяжёлые годы в его жизни. Типичный подростковый период: с родителями плохо, друзей нет, в школе проблемы. После «Через Вселенных» у него ни осталось ни любимой девушки, ни друзей-пауков. Только обычная жизнь: родители, школа, несколько друзей и жизнь Человека-паука. Тем временем, у Гвен-паука тоже очень хорошая, даже местами чуть лучше, чем у Майлза, драматургическая сюжетная арка. Отлично раскрываются отношения Гвен Стейси и её отца, который искренне уверен, что Женщина-паук, которой является Гвен, убила местную версию Питера Паркера. В итоге, оказывается, что существует огромная мультвселенная, в которой вселенные пауков связаны Паутиной Вселенных. Мигель и его общество пауков очень хотят «защищать канон». И в момент жесточайшей битвы, она ссориться с отцом, который узнал её личность, и убегает вместе с другими версиями Человека-паука, в частности с Мигелем (чуть другой версией Человека-паука 2099). Интересно, кстати, сложилась химия отношений Майлза и Гвен. Им действительно веришь. Они выглядят, как хорошая пара-подростков. А ведь им действительно по 15 и 16-17 лет обоим. И когда наступает момент, очень больно они расстаются. Позже оказывается, что Мигель, пытаясь сохранять общие черты сюжета Пауков, хочет допустить смерть отца Майлза, который вот-вот стал капитаном. Типо якобы у Паука должны умирать всегда: Гвен Стейси, друг-капитан полиции и дядя Бэн. Ну, какой-то бред. В целом фильм хороший. Хоть и масштабно противоречит всем версиям Мультивселенной КВМ или «Человека-паука» 1994 года. Конечно, возможно, в этом и прикол, что Мигель врёт, удерживая собственное сообщество, как самопровозглашенную территорию, чтобы не пересекаться с Мадам-Паутиной из «Человека-паука» (1994) или УВИ из сериала «Локи» и типо это раскроется в третьей и финальной части. Например, чета никто не приходил в Киновселенную Марвел исправлять канон, лишь потому-что там не умирал дядя Бэн или не появлялась Гвен Стейси. Или никто не приходил во вселенную Тоби Магуайра, лишь потому-что его Гвен Стейси не умерла и её отец, капитан полиции, тоже не умер. If Into the Spider-Verse felt like a comic book flipped at 24 frames per second, significant stretches of this one felt like it was flipped at 48. The animation is absolutely breathtaking, and the juggling act of all these characters, dimensions, and styles is remarkable, but the film’s constant need to stimulate becomes overstimulating: there’s always music, movement, and something happening in the background, rarely giving you room to breathe. The "Achilles' heel" of the multiverse concept is partly that there’s simply too much going on, and this movie occasionally falls into its own trap. The best parts are when it slows down. The Spot is introduced in an interesting way, but never really gets the one-on-one dynamic with Spider-Man you want from a central villain, partly because the emotional anchor is spread across so many characters that there’s nowhere obvious to attach yourself. It’s a double-edged sword: the concept is strong and the execution is often remarkable, but the emotional center is spread too thin. Still, the set pieces and animation are incredible, and the new dimensions it opens up are exciting. The ending leaves plenty on the table for the next chapter, and I’m excited to see where it goes. It’s still a very good animated film, but I prefer the first one, which somehow managed to balance all of this perfectly.

Achei um filme interessante, mas a princípio fiquei com a sensação de que ele era um pouco raso. Eu estava esperando que algumas coisas fossem mais aprofundadas e, quando terminou, ainda senti que faltava alguma coisa. Mas é um daqueles filmes que continuam na cabeça depois dos créditos. Quanto mais eu pensava, mais percebia as coisas que ele deixa nas entrelinhas. Me chamou atenção como a mão funciona quase como uma metáfora para o vicio. Depois que os personagens experimentam aquele contato, eles passam a querer repetir a experiência cada vez mais, ignorando as possíveis consequências. Não parece ser só um filme sobre espíritos, mas também sobre dependência, impulsividade e a dificuldade de parar quando algo já tomou conta de você. Mia acaba sendo a maior prova disso. Carregando o luto pela mãe, ela se agarra à ilusão de que ainda pode falar com ela, mesmo quando fica evidente que aquilo não é realmente sua mãe. Também achei interessante como o filme trabalha os personagens. Apesar de serem um grupo de amigos, cada um mantém sua individualidade. A Mia, por exemplo, demonstra um carinho pelo Riley durante parte da história, mas, quando surge a possibilidade de conseguir algo que ela queria, ela acaba deixando esse cuidado de lado. No geral, achei uma produção bem feita, com uma boa construção dos personagens e uma atmosfera que funciona muito bem. Não foi um filme que me conquistou de imediato, mas definitivamente me fez pensar depois que terminou.

Considerando sucessos recentes de terror e seus impactos verdadeiros no cinema, como Midsommar, Obsession e A Hora do Mal, três títulos que gosto e aprecio o trabalho de direção, Fale Comigo possuía um aspecto semelhante, talvez pela boa propaganda que sempre tive de alguns veículos da informação que sigo. Adolescentes burros se reúnem para brincar com o que não se deve, usando uma mão decepada como portal pro outro mundo. Aí acontece uma merda e a partir daí, o filme começa a andar em círculos e atirar para todos os lados, quase gritando "me escuta aqui! Eu tenho metáforas pra fazer!" Enquanto não aproveita pra desenvolver de verdade, nada. É uma visão criativa limitada, com uma direção que eu não achei nada demais, e que na minha opinião, precisava de outro segmento e uma interpretação mais simples (talvez até momentânea) para agradar. No entanto, é preciso salientar que esse filme seria sim muito funcional se seu texto fosse mais sincero consigo mesmo, e não uma máquina aleatória de escrever subtramas. O primeiro terço do filme é muito legal e promissor em apresentar uma história simples, no qual o terror adolescente iria valer o seu tempo, mas ao longo do meio e do final, após acontecer o acidente principal na trama, ele se perde em tantas mensagens e o desenvolvimento chato do passado da protagonista. Os personagens são rasos, alguns em atuações bem fraquinhas e em dilemas que você simplesmente não acredita que essa besteirada propõe a discutir. É muito chato acompanhar essa situação dos protagonistas onde nada acontece e eles são poucos punidos pelos problemas que causaram a partir de uma brincadeira errada. Os relacionamentos entre os personagens são somente tristes de acompanhar, e a "tensão romântica", numa tentativa de colocar mais um arco a se desenvolver, é falha e uma das piores coisas do filme A parte gráfica, do body horror, é bem executada, porém me parece jogada na trama apenas para causar impacto. No geral, eu simplesmente não gostei do filme e talvez eu só tenha achado bem bobo e desrespeitoso, pelo tamanho da discussão e mensagem que estavam ali retratando. Esquecível

Um terror da Oceania que foca no abuso da tecnologia ganha espaço no streaming e  no boca boca da Austrália, ganhando ainda mais visibilidade por ter sido distribuída pela A24. Danny e Michael Phillipou dirigem e escrevem a obra sendo a primeira da dupla de irmãos. È evidente que Talk to Me teve como principal influencia a onda da incerteza do que a Tecnologia poderia ocasionar no pós anos 2000, visto em Future Days, ExistenZ e em Pulse (KAIRO) de Kyioshi Kurosawa. A abordagem do  filme ornamenta o titulo da obra, O Fale Comigo, cria a critica ao digital, ao não sentir e o ao não conversar, uma destituição de uma característica humana, mas puxada para uma visão do horror. A obra, influenciada por uma critica a tecnologia, sustenta a ideia do que passou para uma batalha da personagem principal, onde com insônia, as telas do celular viram uma espécie de refugio. Os irmãos Philipou, tomam cuidado para não escancarar a significância do filme, seja na forma poética ou simbológica, aproveitando bem o espaço real, fora do digital. As câmeras dos celulares se  comportam como seres transportadores da alegria, ao mesmo tempo, que os que tem a ferramenta da alegria nas suas mãos, almas vazias e loucas por atenção se mostram, e ai, Talk to Me começa. A obra, se difere da abordagem mais direta do terror ocidental, dando espaço para uma visão mais destoante, essa mesma diferença se comporta de forma fenomenal, mas ai, entra a abordagem da historia, onde a formula da distoancia entre o real e o virtual perde cada vez mais espaço para uma visão mais pé no chão e convencional. Pouco se salva da abordagem de terror desse filme, onde parece mais um filme de terror convencional, tendo como ponto altos, os ótimos ângulos de câmera. A personagem que e o centro da historia, se mete em um buraco sem escapatória, não em forma de ser o que deve ser, mas cansativo. Talk to Me dos irmãos Philipou é  uma carta escrita em papel de ouro, mas extremamente mal escrita com letras iguais, onde a cada paragrafo, não alcança lugar nenhum para querer ser lida.

Talk to Me tem uma premissa muito boa. A ideia de uma mão misteriosa que permite conversar com espíritos é criativa e encaixa muito bem no contexto de um grupo de adolescentes que transforma aquilo em uma brincadeira de festa. O filme também tenta construir um lado mais emocional ao explorar o trauma da Mia após a morte da mãe por suicídio e como isso influencia suas escolhas. O problema é que, para mim, essa parte da história simplesmente não funciona como deveria. Todo o conflito envolvendo o Riley, as consequências de ele usar a mão e a forma como a família passa a culpar a protagonista nunca conseguiu me envolver, então o peso dramático que o roteiro tenta criar acaba se perdendo. As atuações também não ajudam muito. A Sophie Wilde entrega uma boa performance como Mia e consegue carregar boa parte do filme nas costas, mas o restante do elenco passa uma sensação de ser apenas competente, sem interpretações que realmente se destaquem. Mesmo com algumas cenas de horror bem feitas e uma atmosfera desconfortável em certos momentos, fiquei com a impressão de que a execução ficou bem abaixo do potencial da ideia. Em compensação, a maquiagem merece muito destaque. Os ferimentos, as possessões e todo o visual dos espíritos são muito bem feitos e ajudam bastante na imersão, sendo facilmente um dos pontos altos do filme. Apesar disso, o final é, sem dúvida, a melhor parte. A conclusão amarra muito bem a trajetória da Mia e as regras da própria maldição. Ver a protagonista assumindo o lugar de um dos espíritos e sendo invocada por outras pessoas fecha o ciclo de uma forma muito inteligente e dá um novo significado a tudo o que aconteceu antes. É um desfecho forte e memorável, que quase faz o filme terminar melhor do que foi durante boa parte da sua duração. Ainda assim, no geral, Talk to Me acabou sendo uma experiência apenas mediana para mim.

Talk to Me propose un concept de possession particulièrement original grâce à cette mystérieuse main embaumée. J’ai aussi beaucoup aimé l’idée de voir des adolescents transformer une expérience aussi dangereuse en simple jeu, allant même jusqu’à se filmer. Honnêtement, j’ai trouvé cette idée très crédible : si un tel objet existait, il y a de fortes chances que ce soit exactement ce qui arriverait. Le film mise davantage sur le malaise que sur une accumulation de jump scares. Les scènes d’horreur sont brutales, dérangeantes et ponctuées d’un peu de body horror particulièrement efficace, même si elles ne sont finalement pas si nombreuses. Derrière son apparence de film d’épouvante, Talk to Me est avant tout un drame sur le deuil, la solitude et la dépendance. J’ai toutefois trouvé que la première moitié tournait un peu en rond. Le scénario tarde à véritablement décoller et le rythme manque d’équilibre avant que les enjeux prennent enfin de l’ampleur. Les personnages secondaires sont également peu développés, ce qui fait qu’on s’attache rarement à eux. Malgré ces défauts, Talk to Me demeure un film d’horreur original, moderne et efficace qui renouvelle intelligemment le cinéma de possession.

Talk to Me é um daqueles raros filmes de terror que compreende que o género não precisa de escolher entre a substância e o entretenimento. Pode ser profundamente alegórico sem deixar de ser genuinamente assustador. Pode falar sobre luto, dependência e autodestruição sem sacrificar a tensão em nome da mensagem. E é precisamente esse equilíbrio que faz do filme uma das obras mais marcantes do terror contemporâneo. À primeira vista, a sua premissa não parece particularmente inovadora. A possessão enquanto metáfora para o vício, a procura desesperada por uma fuga ao sofrimento e a sedução exercida por forças que prometem alívio imediato são temas que o cinema de terror tem explorado há décadas. No entanto, Talk to Me nunca depende da originalidade da ideia, depende da excelência da sua execução. Os irmãos Philippou demonstram uma confiança invulgar na realização, construindo uma atmosfera opressiva onde cada movimento de câmara, cada corte e cada silêncio contribuem para uma crescente sensação de inevitabilidade. O terror não nasce apenas daquilo que vemos, mas sobretudo da certeza de que a tragédia já começou muito antes de as personagens se aperceberem disso. O maior triunfo do filme reside na forma como recusa transformar a alegoria no seu principal espetáculo. Nos últimos anos, o chamado "elevated horror" tornou-se tão obcecado pelas suas leituras simbólicas que, muitas vezes, se esqueceu de provocar medo. Filmes excessivamente preocupados em explicar o trauma acabam frequentemente por neutralizar aquilo que torna o terror tão poderoso, a irracionalidade, a ansiedade e o desconhecido. Talk to Me faz exatamente o contrário. Primeiro assusta. Só depois convida à interpretação. A metáfora nunca sufoca a experiência, emerge naturalmente dela. A mão funciona como um objeto profundamente simbólico. Não representa apenas o contacto com os mortos, mas também a sedução de qualquer mecanismo de evasão que ofereça prazer imediato à custa da própria destruição. É impossível não estabelecer um paralelo com a dependência, a primeira experiência surge como uma curiosidade, transforma-se rapidamente num ritual coletivo e termina por consumir completamente quem já não consegue distinguir o controlo da ilusão de controlo. O filme evita qualquer moralismo simplista, preferindo mostrar como o sofrimento emocional cria terreno fértil para esse tipo de dependência. Grande parte da força dramática deve-se à extraordinária interpretação de Sophie Wilde. A sua performance nunca procura o exagero característico do cinema de possessão, pelo contrário, assenta numa vulnerabilidade constante que torna a deterioração psicológica da personagem devastadoramente convincente. Wilde consegue transmitir medo, culpa, isolamento, desespero e alienação com uma subtileza impressionante. Mesmo nos momentos mais extremos, nunca sentimos que estamos perante uma personagem, mas perante alguém que perdeu progressivamente a capacidade de distinguir a realidade daquilo que deseja desesperadamente acreditar. Também merece destaque a maturidade visual do filme. A fotografia utiliza uma paleta aparentemente banal para criar um universo onde o sobrenatural invade lentamente a normalidade quotidiana. Os efeitos práticos são utilizados com enorme inteligência, nunca como mero espetáculo grotesco, mas como extensões físicas do sofrimento psicológico das personagens. O design sonoro, por sua vez, torna-se quase uma personagem invisível, amplificando a tensão através de silêncios desconfortáveis e de uma presença constante que parece contaminar todos os espaços. Talvez o aspeto mais admirável seja a forma como os Philippou compreendem a essência do terror. O medo nunca é tratado como uma recompensa momentânea entre cenas de exposição, é uma atmosfera permanente. O filme recusa a estrutura previsível do susto fácil e opta por uma ansiedade lenta, quase insuportável, onde o espectador sente que cada decisão aproxima inevitavelmente as personagens da sua destruição. Infelizmente, existe hoje uma tendência para reduzir qualquer filme de terror que aborde o luto ou o trauma a uma simples tentativa de imitar Hereditary. Essa leitura ignora décadas de história do género. Muito antes disso, obras como Don't Look Now, The Changeling, Pet Sematary, The Orphanage ou The Descent já utilizavam o sobrenatural para explorar o peso da perda. O terror sempre foi uma linguagem privilegiada para falar do sofrimento humano. A diferença está na forma como cada filme escolhe fazê-lo. E Talk to Me escolhe fazê-lo através do medo. Medo genuíno. Daquele que não desaparece quando as luzes da sala se acendem. Daquele que permanece porque compreendemos que os verdadeiros demónios do filme nunca foram apenas os espíritos invocados, mas a facilidade com que o vazio emocional nos leva a abrir a porta a qualquer coisa que prometa preenchê-lo. Poucos filmes recentes conseguiram equilibrar de forma tão elegante o horror visceral, a tragédia íntima e a sofisticação formal. Sem reinventar completamente o género, Talk to Me demonstra que o terror continua a ser um dos meios mais poderosos para explorar aquilo que existe de mais frágil na condição humana. É um filme que assusta primeiro, pensa depois e permanece muito tempo connosco depois dos créditos terminarem.

El Padrino no es una película: es un tratado audiovisual sobre la inevitabilidad del poder, la herencia y la corrupción moral disfrazado de cine de gánsteres. Coppola toma el sueño americano, lo estrangula con una corbata italiana y lo convierte en una tragedia shakespeariana donde la familia funciona simultáneamente como refugio y condena. Lo verdaderamente fascinante no es la violencia, sino la burocracia con la que se ejerce. Michael Corleone no desciende al crimen por ambición, sino por la lógica casi determinista de un sistema donde la ética termina subordinada a la sangre. Cada decisión parece una tesis sobre cómo el poder deja de ser una herramienta para convertirse en una identidad. La fotografía de Gordon Willis, conocida con toda justicia como "el Príncipe de las Tinieblas", no ilumina a los personajes: los juzga. Las sombras no son una elección estética, sino una declaración filosófica de que toda autoridad nace parcialmente oculta. Y Nino Rota compone una partitura que suena menos a música y más a un lamento histórico por una familia condenada desde el primer brindis. Decir que El Padrino es "una película de mafiosos" es como decir que La Odisea trata sobre un hombre que vuelve a casa. Es una reducción casi ofensiva. Lo que Coppola construye es un mito moderno donde el capitalismo, el honor y la violencia dialogan hasta volverse indistinguibles. Obra maestra. No porque sea perfecta, sino porque redefine el lenguaje con el que el cine habla sobre el poder.

Man sollte keine Angst davor haben, Klassiker der Filmgeschichte zu kritisieren, bloß, weil dieser von der Masse gefeiert wird. The Godfather ist so ein Beispiel. Man kann nachvollziehen, wieso er ein großes Publikum erreicht: Der Plot ist gefällig erzählt , die Figuren sind schlicht und die Bildsprache eingängig. Wir verstehen sofort, was Sache ist. Copolla lässt kaum Raum für Ambivalentes, auch Politisches hält er hier vollkommen raus. Dabei kann gerade das Mafia-Genre rasant über die Entstehung von Kapital erzählen, doch das geschieht hier nur randständig. Stattdessen verschafft man dem Publikum Zugang zum Film durch die nervende Betonung von Familienwerten – ja, The Godfather ist ein durch und durch konservativer Film. Die Schwermütigkeit und die Länge des Films ist dabei nicht mit einer anspruchsvollen Kost zu verwechseln. Im Gegenteil kann man es sich immer ganz warm und gemütlich machen, wenn Don Vito Corleone vor dem Bildschirm läuft: Hier wird zwar geschossen und gemordet, aber immerhin ist hier das patriarchale Familienmodell noch intakt. An einem Scoresese-Gangster-Film, geschweige denn an einem Coppola, kommt dieser nicht ran.

A product of its time. So many of the characters were so surface level for a fucking 3 hour long movie! I've unironically seen better character building over the course of 40 minute CW serials. I didn't find even Al Pacino that interesting/endearing, let alone any of the female characters. Don Corleone was the most interesting and complex to me, and I liked him - but unlike Tony Soprano, they didn't care to explore the moral implications and repercussions of his lifestyle. The people we see them kill are Bad and Evil and one-not and he Loves His Children and is Tough But Fair. The pacing was weird - I couldn't tell what the final act was leading up to, and then apparently it was the assassination of some randoms we've had 2 minutes of prior screentime of and who I couldn't feel the symbolic weight of anyways, by anonymous shooters we've never seen before. (That's not to say I didn't greatly enjoy mass-murder-baptism scene - in fact it was probably my favourite, in isolation - and I do appreciate that it represented a greater symbolic act of revenge for his brother's death, but it still didn't work for me.) And then we end with a brooding Al Pacino lying to his girlfriend who has no personality besides Pretty and I did not care about, and therefore fully adopting the new "don" role, becoming the new Godfather. And then a door slams. I guess. As the credits were rolling I was just left thinking... that's it? Where was the fallout, the consequences, for all that death and drama? Please, just one meaningful consequence? This pacing can only be justified if they were always intending on making a "Part II" to continue the story, because on its own it just feels incomplete to me. It was undeniably cinematically well-made and I recognise probably, to me, a victim of the "classic movie which was ground breaking and iconic for the time and was the first to do all these cool things that have now been done better a million times over and I take for granted" problem. Same as "Taxi Driver". But I'm not a film critic, I'm only going to review a movie taken on its own merit, and to me... I don't know. The themes were interesting...? I guess? The idea of Business getting conflated with the Personal was a throughline. Again, I've seen the revenge plot done better since. I recall enjoying the first part - the plot was well set up and the villains mysterious and threatening. But then they all just... die. With the fall-out captured in a five minute long montage of newspaper headlines. New villains appear, and then they die too. And this valiant "that's my familys work not mine" war hero just... flips, and becomes a mafioso the second he gets back from like a month max of exile in Italy where the most significant thing he did was watch his Italian wife get blown up in a car for no reason after having genuinely more dialogue with her father than her and then immediately forgetting about her. There's no consequences, no explicit moral reckoning, for what was supposed to be that climatic act of killing the men who shot his father earlier in the film. He doesn't even have one panic attack! The battered sister is used as a plot point and a pawn to advance the more important sophisticated business of mafia men. Even at the end when she's hysterically yelling at Pacino "you never even considered me [when you killed my abusive husband]" it's like... yeah, he didn't, in multiple ways. If he wasn't aware of his violence, he didn't care how she'd be affected by losing her loving husband, and if he was aware of his violence, that wasn't even the reason he killed him! He didn't care that she was being abused, he cared that he was part of some complex behind-the-scenes murder plot of him. That never went anywhere because everyone gets killed! Like, I get it. It was the 50s, who cares about women, but why include DV as a plot point - going so far as to have a too-long scene of a man chasing his pregnant wife around their house with a belt while she screams, and then beating her - and then just stomp on it? Maybe that was the point, that by the end of the film Pacino is just so far gone into the moral grey of the mob that he doesn't care and that's a bad thing. That would make it more interesting, but not necessarily better. He is explicitly positioned as the protagonist and yet shows so few positive qualities throughout the whole film. I just don't buy his character degradation, if that was the intention. These flat, tired depictions of women just cheapen any movie they're in. If you zoom out, you realise all you're watching is the product of a bunch of white men sitting around in a room talking about a bunch of white men sitting around in a room talking. Just jerk eachother off already. We want to believe the Author is this unbiased surveyor and imitator of the human condition, and that reckoning - it brings them down to earth for me. How brilliant can a man or his story be if they don't trascend or even attempt to transcend the cruelty and primitivism of their era? Oh well. It's fun to get all the Sopranos references now. Maybe watching that first was setting this film up for failure because there's so much more room over 6 seasons and 50+ hours for real, conscientious character development and moral complexity and getting attached to not just the people but the world being built, than a movie, even one as long as this. I should watch this again.

Well, “Leave the gun, take the cannolis ” is now officially my favorite line ever from a film. I love being part Italian so I can “claim” just a sliver of the vibes of this movie. I know these are quintessential movies, so I am so excited to finally watch the first part, but having just read the original book by Mario Puzo, I am left with three main takeaways: 1. This is a Peter Jackson, LOTR book adaptation level. Some scenes are truly ripped out the pages and shot exactly as they are written. Coppola consulted closely with Puzo and that shows. 2. Like most book to movie adaptations, I really do prefer the book to the movie. There is so much to love about the film. The acting is superb and so many scenes are beautifully shot, but so much of the context that I loved from reading the book is lost in translation. 3. For the second time this past month, I have watched a film based on a book that I really loved and appreciated. The first is the Odyssey and now the Godfather. Both movies I really loved, but my love for the ethos and deeper story in the written world makes me still feel like something is missing in the film. Both are still almost 3 hour movies, yet they felt so fast and are almost rushed in a way. I want to stay with Michael’s slow build into becoming a part of the family business. I want to see the full return of Odysseus to Ithaca and for it to feel the full completion and vindication. I know the mediums are different but I think these are connected in my mind and are resulting in me not feeling like they are “perfect” films. Still, this was an excellent watch, but my biggest recommendation is to read a copy of the book.

We know from Gay Talese’s book Honor Thy Father that being a professional mobster isn’t all sunshine and roses. More often, it’s the boredom of stuffy rooms and a bad diet of carry-out food, punctuated by brief, terrible bursts of violence. This is exactly the feel of “The Godfather,” which brushes aside the flashy glamour of the traditional gangster picture and gives us what’s left: fierce tribal loyalties, deadly little neighborhood quarrels in Brooklyn, and a form of vengeance to match every affront. The remarkable thing about Mario Puzo’s novel was the way it seemed to be told from the inside out; he didn’t give us a world of international intrigue, but a private club as constricted as the seventh grade. Everybody knew everybody else and had a pretty shrewd hunch what they were up to. The movie (based on a script labored over for some time by Puzo and then finally given form, I suspect, by director Francis Ford Coppola) gets the same feel. We tend to identify with Don Corleone’s family not because we dig gang wars, but because we have been with them from the beginning, watching them wait for battle while sitting at the kitchen table and eating chow mein out of paper cartons. “The Godfather” himself is not even the central character in the drama. That position goes to the youngest, brightest son, Michael, who understands the nature of his father’s position while revising his old-fashioned ways. The Godfather’s role in the family enterprise is described by his name; he stands outside the next generation which will carry on and, hopefully, angle the family into legitimate enterprises. Those who have read the novel may be surprised to find Michael at the center of the movie, instead of Don Corleone. In fact, this is simply an economical way for Coppola to get at the heart of the Puzo story, which dealt with the transfer of power within the family. Marlon Brando, who plays the Godfather as a shrewd, unbreakable old man, actually has the character lead in the movie; Al Pacino, with a brilliantly developed performance as Michael, is the lead. But Brando’s performance is a skillful throwaway, even though it earned him an Academy Award for best actor. His voice is wheezy and whispery, and his physical movements deliberately lack precision; the effect is of a man so accustomed to power that he no longer needs to remind others. Brando does look the part of old Don Corleone, mostly because of acting and partly because of the makeup, although he seems to have stuffed a little too much cotton into his jowls, making his lower face immobile. The rest of the actors supply one example after another of inspired casting. Although “The Godfather” is a long, minutely detailed movie of some three hours, there naturally isn’t time to go into the backgrounds and identities of such characters as Clemenza, the family lieutenant; Jack Woltz, the movie czar; Luca Brasi, the loyal professional killer; McCluskey, the crooked cop; and the rest. Coppola and producer Al Ruddy skirt this problem with understated typecasting. As the Irish cop, for example, they simply slide in Sterling Hayden and let the character go about his business. Richard Castellano is an unshakable Clemenza. John Marley makes a perfectly hateful Hollywood mogul (and, yes, he still wakes up to find he’ll have to cancel his day at the races). The success of “The Godfather” as a novel was largely due to a series of unforgettable scenes. Puzo is a good storyteller, but no great shakes as a writer. The movie gives almost everything in the novel except the gynecological repair job. It doesn’t miss a single killing; it opens with the wedding of Don Corleone’s daughter (and attendant upstairs activity); and there are the right number of auto bombs, double crosses, and garrotings. Coppola has found a style and a visual look for all this material so “The Godfather” becomes something of a rarity: a really good movie squeezed from a bestseller. The decision to shoot everything in period decor (the middle and late 1940s) was crucial; if they’d tried to save money as they originally planned, by bringing everything up-to-date, the movie simply wouldn’t have worked. But it’s uncannily successful as a period piece, filled with sleek, bulging limousines and postwar fedoras. Coppola and his cinematographer, Gordon Willis, also do some interesting things with the color photography. The earlier scenes have a reddish-brown tint, slightly overexposed and feeling like nothing so much as a 1946 newspaper rotogravure supplement. Although the movie is three hours long, it absorbs us so effectively it never has to hurry. There is something in the measured passage of time as Don Corleone hands over his reins of power that would have made a shorter, faster moving film unseemly. Even at this length, there are characters in relationships you can’t quite understand unless you’ve read the novel. Or perhaps you can, just by the way the characters look at each other.

Portuguese & English review Portuguese- Tarantino nunca conseguiu chegar a fazer um bom western nas suas tentativas, acaba por não haver uma compreensão de que o seu género de filmar quer realmente chegar ao com Django Unchained e The Hateful Eight, não há realmente uma correlação ou sensatez na utilização do Spaghetti Western. ​O grande problema destas tentativas de Tarantino, tanto em Django Unchained (2012) de forma mais gritante, como em The Hateful Eight, é que o realizador parece acreditar que fazer um Spaghetti Western se resume a decalcar a banda sonora de Ennio Morricone, usar lentes anamórficas de 70mm, filmar planos de pormenor de armas a saírem do coldre e carregar na violência hiperbolizada. Há uma total ausência de correlação e sensatez na utilização do género. O Spaghetti Western original aquele de Sergio Leone, Sergio Corbucci ou Giulio Questi nunca foi apenas sobre o estilo ou sobre "gajos fixes a disparar" era um cinema de urgência, seco, operático, que nascia de uma profunda desilusão do pós-guerra europeu, onde a violência era o reflexo de um mundo desprovido de Deus, de leis e de pátria, onde o silêncio e o deserto falavam mais do que os diálogos. ​Tarantino faz exatamente o oposto: ele sufoca o Western com o seu próprio estilo de filmar, transformando o que deveria ser um género visceral num exercício de autocomplacência verbal. The Hateful Eight falha na raiz porque renega o espaço do Western para se fechar numa peça de teatro filmada, claustrofóbica e tagarela, onde a dinâmica de "quem é quem" dentro duma cabana de neve se assemelha mais a um mistério de Agatha Christie reescrito com palavrões do que à crueza mítica de um clássico da fronteira. As personagens não são anti-heróis ambíguos e fascinantes na linha dos clássicos são apenas bonecos de cartão-canelado, odiosos e cínicos por decreto, criados para debitar monólogos intermináveis que tentam soar profundos mas que apenas revelam um realizador refém do seu próprio maneirismo. ​Não há sensatez moral na violência de Tarantino aqui. Enquanto no Spaghetti Western a brutalidade era trágica, suja e pesada, em The Hateful Eight ela torna-se meramente recreativa, um espetáculo gore gratuito e niilista que perde toda a força catártica. Ao tentar fundir a herança política da Guerra Civil Americana com o cinismo do Western europeu, Tarantino acaba por não chegar a lado nenhum. O filme arrasta-se num ritmo indulgente de três horas, onde a tensão nunca se traduz em peso dramático real, apenas numa contagem de corpos previsível. É o cinema transformado num parque de diversões temático para o próprio realizador, provando que, para se fazer um bom Western, não basta ter em arquivo uma gigantesca coleção de referências; é preciso compreender a mecânica do silêncio, a solidão do horizonte e a gravidade de um corpo que tomba no chão. Ainda um pouco melhor que Django Unchained. English- Tarantino never managed to make a good Western in his attempts, ultimately failing to understand what his genre of filmmaking really wants to achieve with Django Unchained and The Hateful Eight; there's really no correlation or common sense in the use of the Spaghetti Western. The big problem with Tarantino's attempts, both in Django Unchained (2012), most glaringly, and in The Hateful Eight, is that the director seems to believe that making a Spaghetti Western boils down to using Ennio Morricone's soundtrack, employing 70mm anamorphic lenses, filming close-ups of guns being drawn from holsters, and relying heavily on hyperbolized violence. There is a total lack of correlation and wisdom in the use of the genre. The original Spaghetti Western, the one by Sergio Leone, Sergio Corbucci, or Giulio Questi, was never just about style or "nice guys shooting." It was a cinema of urgency, dry, operatic, born from a profound disillusionment with postwar Europe, where violence reflected a world devoid of God, laws, and homeland, where silence and the desert spoke louder than dialogue. Tarantino does the exact opposite: he suffocates the Western with his own filming style, transforming what should be a visceral genre into an exercise in verbal self-indulgence. The Hateful Eight fails at its core because it rejects the space of the Western to enclose itself in a filmed, claustrophobic, and chatty play, where the "who's who" dynamic inside a snow cabin resembles more an Agatha Christie mystery rewritten with profanity than the mythical rawness of a frontier classic. The characters are not ambiguous and fascinating anti-heroes in the vein of the classics; they are merely corrugated cardboard puppets, hateful and cynical by decree, created to deliver endless monologues that attempt to sound profound but only reveal a director held hostage by his own mannerisms. There is no moral sense in Tarantino's violence here. While in the Spaghetti Western the brutality was tragic, dirty, and heavy, in The Hateful Eight it becomes merely recreational, a gratuitous and nihilistic gore spectacle that loses all cathartic force. In trying to merge the political legacy of the American Civil War with the cynicism of the European Western, Tarantino ends up getting nowhere. The film drags on at an indulgent three-hour pace, where the tension never translates into real dramatic weight, just a predictable body count. It is cinema transformed into a theme park for the director himself, proving that, to make a good Western, it is not enough to have a gigantic collection of references in the archives; It's necessary to understand the mechanics of silence, the solitude of the horizon, and the gravity of a body falling to the ground. Still a little better than Django Unchained.

Samuel L Jackson and Walton Goggins deliver great performances, the scope cinematography is excellent and Ennio Morricone’s music from The Thing and others is used to great effect. But I didn’t like this any more than the last time I saw it, which was in the cinema on release. It doesn’t hold together like other Tarantino movies for me, and the stylistic choices (particularly the director’s deliberately intrusive voiceover after the intermission) often come across as smug rather than clever. The worst thing is the way it wears its misogyny on its sleeve, not helped by the presence of the Weinstein name and logo all over the credits. It’s inspired by classic westerns of the 60s and 70s that have clearly racist and misogynistic moments… but those films were made over 50 years ago. This is from 2015 (although that’s a lifetime away in some respects). The use of slur words is extreme, even for Tarantino, and the final scene so grotesque that it overshadows anything good that came before. I don’t know anymore if it’s okay to admire the craft of a film if you find so much of the content repulsive.

Apparently unpopular opinion, but I really didn't like this movie. This movie truly felt like it was six hours long. It was a real chore to sit through. I don't mind dialogue driven films, but the dialogue has to actually be interesting and compelling. It should be additive and purposeful. But here it was mundane and repetitive. It felt like there were multiple conversations that just kept repeating themselves just with different people. Most of these conversations served no real purpose. I'd say a lot of scenes in general even beyond just the dialogue felt pointless. Every scene felt like it was lasting too long. I really did not need to see 10 different scenes of them nailing the door shut. I get it, the door is broken. Nor did I need to see the origin story for said broken door. I really didn't care how it broke. I get what the film was trying to do. It was trying to slowly build tension between everyone until it boils over and turns into a big brawl by the end. But the problem is I never felt this tension. First of all because I never cared about a single character in this movie. There was not a single person I was rooting for. But also because everything was so drawn out any tension that is built up runs out of steam and lost the tension for me because I just wanted them to get on with it. Characters choices just didn't often make sense either. But they had to do things to make it as drawn out as humanly possible. The film was well acted though, I would acknowledge that, at least from most people. Samuel L Jackson does a great job in particular. He probably has the best lines. The ones that actually feel like they mattered. So I don't think the film is without merit whatsoever. But there wasn't a moment in the film where I just was ready for the film to be over already.

Sadly there's just a little too much of that over the top flavor that muddles the enjoyability for me, it ends up being less than the sum of its parts. QT’s There Will Be Blood, a violent, sadistic Western that amounts to something like an origin myth. It is easily his most alienating, least likable movie, and it competes with Django Unchained as his worst. It is baggy, self-indulgent, undisciplined filmmaking. You can sense the willful perversity behind it: It’s almost like a self-imposed challenge — how to make a 2-hour, 45-minute epic in the confines of a single location. (He fails his own challenge.) But despite my reservations, the go-for-broke, don’t-give-a-shit folly of it all earns respect, if not admiration. He knows exactly what he’s doing. I think he knows that there is not a single likable person here (see the title), that the violence is as over-the-top as it’s been in any of his movies, and that he’s pushing the limits of audience patience. He thinks his voice, his talent, his virtuosity, the power of his message, and his audience’s loyalty will carry him through. They don’t, not all the way at least.

Le risque de développer un style de mise en scène est à la longue de s'enfermer dedans et d'en être prisonnier. Peut être que certains esprits plus fermés et ayant une très grande confiance en eux sont moins propices à la remise en question et aux changements propres à la curiosité, ce qui en découle une certaine stagnation quel que soit ce que l'on fait. Ça fait 30 ans que Tarantino répète les mêmes schémas qu'ils narratifs ou dans sa mise en scène. Déjà très marqués dès Pulp fiction, j'ai l'impression que l'on atteint le plus haut dans Kill Bill. Depuis j'ai cette sensation de plus en plus présente dès Inglorious Bastard de revoir les mêmes mécaniques avec seul un décors en toile de fond qui changeait. Si dans ce dernier, cela passait encore, cette impression dérangeante s'est accentuée dans Jango. Ici avec Hateful Eight, cela en est presque une caricature de son propre style, tout devient trop un Déjà Vu et même les dialogues, souvent riches chez Tarantino sont un peu en deçà. Le film demeure agréable et sympathique mais je certaine lassitude l'emporte. Il a néanmoins rompu avec ce style avec Once upon a Time in Hollywood, ce que j'avais apprécié, même si il s'est rappelé à lui même dans les 15 dernieres minutes.

Wow, this movie is something else. I honestly didn't know what to expect going into The Hateful Eight, but I ended up really enjoying it. The movie is pretty slow at first, but I think that's what makes it work. Most of it takes place inside one cabin, with a bunch of strangers who don't trust each other. As the movie goes on, you start questioning everyone and wondering who's actually telling the truth. The line “I’m gonna get you” really fits the feeling of the movie because you constantly feel like someone is about to turn on someone else. The dialogue is probably my favorite part. There isn't always a lot happening, but the conversations are so interesting that I didn't really mind. Tarantino can make people sitting around a table talking feel more intense than an action scene. The characters are constantly trying to figure each other out, and that paranoia keeps building. I also really liked the setting. The snow and the huge amount of isolation make the whole movie feel trapped. They're stuck together with nowhere to go, which makes the tension even better. The cabin almost feels like its own character. The characters are also just crazy 😭. Pretty much everyone is a terrible person in some way, so you don't really know who to root for. Like the movie says, “No one’s gonna be leaving this place alive.” At that point, you already know things are about to go completely off the rails. Overall, The Hateful Eight is definitely a slow burn, but once it gets going, it's really entertaining. The dialogue, characters, setting, and mystery all work together really well. It's definitely worth watching if you're into Tarantino movies.

Filmlerindeki o retro hava, nostaljik film vibeı, hikayeyi kitap okur gibi bölümlere ayrılması, hikaye akışında kronolojik sırayı bozup heyecan verici unsurları yayması ve özellikle filmin sonuna yerleştirmesi onu ayıran özellikleri bence. Ayrıca mizahı da çok iyi. Gerçekten bu adamın özellikle eski kovboy filmlerinin hastası olduğunu ve filmlerinde her alanda o eski, nostaljik havayı vermeye çalıştığına eminim. Öyle ki filmin opening ve ending kısmındaki akan yazıların kabartması ve puntosu bile eskiyi çağrıştırıyor. Ve film içerisindeki şakalar da o filmlerden çıkmış gibi, sadece eski film kasıntılığından uzak oluşu filmin mizah seviyesini yerinde, gülünebilir kılıyor. Bu filmin tek kötü yanı hikayenin kapsamlı olmayışı ve üç saat boyunca aynı mekanda olayları izlememiz. Ancak dediğim gibi söz konusu Tarantino filmi keyifli kılmayı biliyor. Adam hiç sanat sepet işlerine girmeden yalnızca keyif vermek üzerine mükemmel filmler ortaya koyuyor. Ancak bu filmde prensiplerinden birine rastlamamak üzmese de şaşırttı beni: filmde ayak yoktu. Bu alışıla gelmiş bir şey değil Tarantino için ama beni bağlayan bir sorun değil. Neyse son bir film daha kaldı Tarantinodan izleyeceğim sonra bu adamın külliyatı bitecek. Yazmayı unuttum film aynı RDR havası veriyor.

What makes Tarantino one of the greatest storytellers and movie writers is the build-up for the characters, It doesn't matter who the actor playing that character, whether he is a box office star or a rookie, what matter is the character.

The Hateful Eight is basically Tarantino locking a bunch of horrible people in one room and letting them slowly turn on each other, and I love how nasty it gets. Samuel L. Jackson is brilliant, Walton Goggins is probably the funniest person in the film and Jennifer Jason Leigh gives one of the most memorable performances just by sitting there looking completely unhinged. The snowy setting and Ennio Morricone score make the whole thing feel claustrophobic as fuck even though the film is shot on this massive format. I’d put it above a 3.5 because the dialogue, performances and tension make such a simple setup genuinely gripping. I stop at 4 because it’s very long, deliberately slow and the second half gets so violent and over-the-top that some of the mystery gets lost underneath all the chaos

Walter Goggins, before he became famous, coming to understand that his black and white, good bad narrative he’s clung to for so long just isn’t reality. Kurt Russell’s arrogance. I do rather like The Hateful Eight, but it is my least favorite Tarantino film. While it is very violent, it almost feels goofy compared to some of his other movies (especially his earlier movies which often have real darkness and depth to them), and really leans into his more playful side, with comically over the top dialogue and blood, silly voiceovers and slow-motion effects, and a more laid-back vibe than his usual movies that feel like they have a lot more gravitas. This is my first time watching it, but I do feel like I will find this to be QT's least rewatchable film. I love how you can run his movies back and enjoy them just as much, if not more, the second time, but with this one I don't think I'll be compelled to return to it as much, largely because it's just a weaker, far more self-indulgent and dialogue-heavy movie than most of his other films, but all the characters are pretty much awful people (except Zoe Bell's minor character, love her), so there's not really anyone to root for in the movie. I don't know, I did really enjoy The Hateful 8 but it's definitely his least compelling film. I loved the wintry cinematography and remote cabin setting, and the variation of characters and performances, especially Walton Goggins and Jennifer Jason Leigh, but while it is quite enjoyable and a perfectly good western, it's Tarantino's least serious and worst movie.

Et voilà enfin le dernier Tarentino, normalement, d'après ses dires, le dernier, dernier! On verra s'il respecte ce qu'il a dit par le passé. Bref, revenons à nos moutons. La bande-annonce laissait présager du meilleur puisque elle laisse entrevoir une situation de huis-clos, avec une tripotée de personnages haut en couleurs et armés jusqu'aux dents, ce qui, dans ses précédents films nous offre toujours des scènes d'anthologie. Premier constat, 2h45, c'est un peu long. On attend un peu trop de temps pour que le film démarre vraiment, puis le rythme s'accélère, s'emballe carrément, pour partir en vrille totale dans la dernière demi-heure. Finalement, le rythme assez lent du début se comprend car on est scotché par cette accélération progressive qui, si elle avait pu tenir en 30' maximum, Tarentino a la classe et la maîtrise de le faire sur presque 3h. Une très bonne production qui est un plaisir à regarder, mais peut-être pas à revoir, ne serait-ce que pour découvrir d'autres détails supplémentaires liés à la résolution finale.

One of Tarantino’s more underrated films, which is sad because this is him at his peak. A bunch of dudes sitting around talking to each other for two hours as tensions slowly build, capped off with a rather violent ending sequence. What more could you want? The build here is great, I’m glued to my screen waiting for the first pin to drop. But once it does, I found less of a reason to stay invested before having to sit through 20 minutes of building up the backstory. Realizing that no one was going to make it out of this alive, I found myself not as worried about the outcome. I think it’d be cooler if there were a few more twists and turns along the way, maybe having half the group have the same end goal wasn’t the best idea. But, still a very solid film nonetheless. The winter theme and cottage vibes make for a surprisingly cozy watch. I’d love to watch this around Christmas time, hot cocoa in hand (minus the poison). I’m glad that in the end, a union and confederate soldier were able to come together and unite over their hatred for women (satire… slightly).

It’s still pretty far from being one of my favorite Tarantino films - but it’s still a great reminder of why I love his films.

I gave The Hateful Eight 4,5 out of 5 stars because I think it’s a masterpiece. This was such a well-rounded story to watch. I think what made this movie stand out to me, and therefore Tarantino’s style to me, is his chapter by chapter presentation of the film. Well, it is easy to label things up to an episodic format throughout the movie, but Tarantino’s dialogue and cinematography are straight out of a book. I could literally imagine a novel being written as I watched the movie with the grand details that Tarantino’s shots offer in addition to the character dynamics and the insane performances the cast displays throughout the movie. Getting to know the characters and the setting was entertaining, although some monologues and sequences may feel a bit of a drag, it didn’t hamper my attention enough and the movie always kept me at bay. This is the fourth movie I have watched from Tarantino, and this is probably the best one so far.

Auf dieses Nachbartreffen kann man getrost verzichten, denn: Anstrengend, aber im negativen wie nervigen Sinne. Kein Vorwurf an den Cast: Alle Vier merkt man die Spielfreude sichtlich an und ist neben der flotten Inszenierung stellenweise auch ansteckend, nur bleiben ihre Figuren zu uninteressant bzw im Falle von Joe und Angela (Wilde, Rogen) fragt man sich, warum die Ehe bisher so lange gehalten hat und andersrum, die biblische Geduld von Piña und Hawk (Cruz, Norton), denn jede:r hätte nach spätestens 15 Minuten bei der (passiv-)aggressiven Stimmung das Weite gesucht. Aber Olivia Wilde setzt weniger auf Glaubwürdigkeit, sondern mehr auf Übertriebenheit und das von Beginn an: Kaum ein Dialog oder Gestik kommt in dem mit unzähligen Sticheleien versehenen Schlagabtausch ohne Hysterie und Theatralik aus. Subilität hat Sendepause und mit Authenzität hat das auch nicht mehr viel zu tun. Sinnbildlich der Score, der die Gefühlslagen stets (über-)präsent sowie penetrant mit schiefen oder sanften Klangteppichen ausrollt. Später, wenn Wilde den Fokus hinter der (bröckelnden) Fassade blicken möchte, bleibt dieser auch verschüchtert. Wer A sagt, muss auch B sagen: Wilde bleibt bei A brav hängen. Allein nur explizit über sexuelle Vorlieben sprechen, ist halt lange nicht mutig genug, provokant erst recht nicht. Entsprechend gestaltet sich Eskalation ernüchternd inkonsequent, noch weniger entlarvend. Stattdessen werden dabei doch wieder die platten Gags rausgeholt. Das ist nicht pointiert, sondern peinlich. Die Komplexität der Konflikte um verschiedene Beziehungsformen und Liebe, aber auch Kommunikationsunfähigkeit, entfaltet sich dadurch selten schlagkräftig, auch da der Film lediglich auf konstruierte Zuspitzung aus ist. Am Ende stehen dann doch wieder Luxusprobleme im Vordergrund und die Tatsache, dass bei aller Offenheit andere Partnerschaftsmodelle außerhalb der traditionellen Ehe, doch nur pervertiert sind und Unruhe reinbringen. Ahja... Aber dann, die letzten 5 Minuten: Die sind plötzlich zutiefst menschlich. Olivia Wilde findet in der Ruhe nochmal leise Töne, die stark beeindrucken! Gerade hier ist zu spüren, was für ein reizvolles Potenzial 'The Invite' besitzt. Hätte sich der Film in den vorherigen 100 Minuten doch mal mehr aus der zahmen (Hollywood-)Komfortzone getraut.

This film attempts to be a serious drama with relationships meant to be taken seriously but is quickly undermined by forced comedic beats that are not effective. Ed Norton's monologue, for example, is extremely pretentious and while it might’ve worked in a play, comes across as a dismissible, out-of-place punchline. Each character was unlikeable to some degree. The performances themselves were also lacking, where it feels overdone and lacking any sort of chemistry or desire- which the story is attempting to revolve itself around. This quickly becomes repetitive and one-note during key moments. Some positives- the bottle setting is a perfect choice, and includes some creative shots. Overall, this was a film that was difficult to connect. It was difficult to connect with the toxic relationship dynamics, forgettable overblown performances, unlikeable characters, and a story that wants you to take it seriously but is undermined by the overdone comedy.

I was quite surprised by this one, especially being that I’m not really a Seth Rogan fan and I thought that pairing him with Olivia Wilde would be rather odd.  However, besides his annoying laugh at the very beginning of the film, Rogan turned in a really good performance as Joe, the closet musician who gave up his dream of being in an alternative band for a job as a music teacher at a community college so he could provide some form of security for his wife and daughter.  Angela, Olivia Wilde, the wife and stay-at-home mom has a spending problem and suffers from OCD.  Their sex life is null. And then there are their neighbors from upstairs, who sound like their sex life is amazing as it echoes through the ceiling.  Angela invites them over for dinner/house warming and that’s when the story truly unfolds as Hawk, portrayed mysteriously by Edward Norton, and Piná, played with enthusiastic vigor by Penelope Cruz, bring an honest sense of openness into the picture. Oh…there’s definitely a twist!  And the ending is quite…comforting? Good movie.  Bound to make you think about your relationship.

También es la primera vez que veo a Penélope Cruz y me gustó mucho su actuación. Seth Rogen actua bastante bien y Edward Norton también. Ok so I lost my shades watching this but it was worth it! I went into this movie not knowing anything and can confidently say that's the best way to watch. The dialogue is fantastic and a lot of the comedy in this movie comes from shock value in regards to said dialogue. The performances of the cast were so genuine and human, it felt like the actors embodied characters that resemble everyday people. I believe that part of the reason this film is so strong is that the interactions and characters feel so familiar to us. We as viewers can all relate in multiple facets to these people, a testament to how good the writing was here. The film is limited in regards to its setting but that's actually not a bad thing here. In sum, this movie takes some surprising turns so try to go in blind if you can!

Strange things are afoot in THE INVITE. I love movies that are basically just a play. Ed Norton was my saving grace, actually; he's always sweeping in with a random comment to help ease the tension. I hope this gets some Oscar noms (it would actually be so sweet to see Seth Rogen nominated in a serious acting category).

I wouldn’t be surprised if The Invite finds its way into multiple Oscar conversations. I already complimented my favorite aspects in my first review, but man, everything was so well done here. Today’s audience really liked the humor and I think Seth Rogen in particular balanced everything so well, including the humor and facial expressions. Being able to pull off a combination of one of the funniest and most tense movies of the year is special. The way they filmed it — the artsy opening sequence (which also perfectly comes full circle with the ending), the camera/lens choices, the color grading, and the way they framed the characters and utilized foreground and background blur — was so good. The color coordination too. I love how the opening scene goes from them being happy at an undisclosed time to the beautiful frames of Joe just being miserable. This film is an excellent psychological study on self and marriage — communication, opening up, your perspective on the things you have, and resentment. Joe had so many good things going for him, between his daughter, kids learning from him, his musical talent, a pretty wife, and a nice home in San Francisco. He chose to be hung up on the past and push people away. Angela just had communication issues and made Joe feel unheard. You also see that the seemingly perfect couple indeed had their own issues, but Hawk was able to apologize when he was wrong and it was easier for him to be vulnerable. It also just shows how someone like him — someone you could easily judge or put into a box because of his sex life — had his own life experiences that you could empathize with. The end is beautiful because music can really break down barriers and be a language of its own.

no sé ni por donde empezar. dramática, graciosa, humana y con un final… esta opinión no tiene spoilers. la película podría haberse decidido por quedarse solo en la comedia, que lo estaba haciendo a la perfección, pero decide dar un pasó más y agregarle un peso psicológico simplemente deslumbrante. la construcción de toda la historia, para mí, es perfecta. comenzando desde el uso de unos planos súper inteligentes que demuestran desde el primer minuto esa separación “invisible” entre sus protagonistas, algo similar a lo que sucede en parasite (2019) para diferenciar las clases sociales. sumándole a eso una tensión que es genuinamente palpable desde el momento en el que Joe pisa la casa por primera vez, y por último la introducción de cada personaje en escena. la escritura de cada personaje (valga la redundancia) es, en mi opinión, donde radica toda la magia de la película. todos tienen una profundidad terrible, algunos lo demuestran explícitamente en sus diálogos, otros con miradas y algunos simplemente bailando o tocando un piano. pero el hecho de conectar con todos ellos me voló la cabeza, entendes al personaje de Joe y porque reacciona como lo hace, lo mismo su esposa y sus maravillosos vecinos. y esto no lo hacen de una manera brusca, lo hacen entre chistes, entre simples comentarios, y de apoco, sin darte cuenta, conoces de pie a cabeza a todos los que están en esa habitación. es fascinante como pasa de ser una comedia negra, incluso incómoda en varias ocasiones, a un drama psicológico que te lleva a las lagrimas. ¿como un personaje que te hizo reír tanto podría estar tan roto por dentro? ¿como una casa tan perfecta oculta tanto enojo, tristeza y vacío? y destaco particularmente ese detalle de “casa perfecta” porque todo el tiempo se encargan de alagarla, demostrar el esfuerzo que ponen en los detalles, pero todo indica un nivel de superficialidad terrible, demostrado explícitamente en el momento que nos damos cuenta que solo está bien lo que se ve a simple vista, salvo su habitación, su lugar mas personal… al igual que con el drama (2026) que destaque su gran trabajo para representar el sobrepensar, acá debo destacar el increíble trabajo que hacen con la ansiedad y las inseguridades que cargamos con nosotros mismos. la importancia que tiene el amarnos, el sentirnos cómodos en el cuerpo que cargamos y no solo en nuestro físico, sino abrazar nuestros errores, nuestros sueños frustrados, e incluso nuestra infelicidad en muchas ocasiones. y esto no solo por nuestro bien, no solo para que no vivamos miserablemente, sino que estamos tan cegados por nuestro propio odio, que no vemos como estamos lastimando a la persona que mas amamos. si esto lo vivis o lo viviste en primera persona (como yo) pega todo el doble de fuerte, especialmente la angustia que carga el personaje de Joe y Angela. y esta pregunta… ¿como vamos a pedir que nos amen, que nos deseen, si ni nosotros mismos podemos vernos al espejo? todo esto tratado desde el humor, desde la sátira, todo construido lentamente para un final que te parte al medio. ESE momento, un cierre perfecto. lo que destacaría por sobre todas estas cosas es como logran trabajar las inseguridades de AMBOS de igual manera, no odias a uno y amas a otro, entendes a los dos. y eso, aparte de por la gran escritura que tienen y la dirección SUBLIME de Olivia Wilde, es por el enorme peso interpretativo que hay en sus actores, de verdad, lo que hace Seth Rogen y Ella es digno de todas las premiaciones. Penélope Cruz y Edward Norton están espectaculares también. especialmente Norton nos regala la escena en la que vemos el primer quiebre de la película, el momento exacto donde pasa de ser una comedia a un drama TOTAL. y que el personaje de Penélope sea psiquiatra y sexóloga, le da un peso enorme a cada diálogo, e indirectamente nos hacen prestarle más atención a absolutamente todo lo que nos cuenta. un uso espectacular de ambas profesiones. cómo logran ocultar diálogos tristísimos entre carcajadas es digno de pararse y aplaudir. la importancia que pueden tener unos simples tragos, un tequila, un vino, un flan, de cada detalle sacas una lectura, no hay absolutamente nada puesto al azar. busca incomodar, pero te agarra desprevenido. te hace reir, pero al mismo tiempo te hace llorar, te distrae, pero al mismo tiempo te hace mirar para adentro y llevarnos a corregir muchos errores que llevamos con nosotros día a día… y como estos mismos no solo nos arruinan a nosotros, sino que también a las personas que más amamos. me pareció de verdad una película enorme, me encanta como están tratando temas tan psicológicos en el cine actual, como están buscando esa conexión con el espectador y, personalmente, la están logrando al 100%. me dejó sin aliento, pensaba reírme toda la película y termine destruido. todavía me da vergüenza escribir lo que pienso, perdón si me dejo llevar demasiado, es todo realmente pura sinceridad, si otros no conectaron o simplemente no les gustó, esta perfecto también. yo la viví así.

In Gladiator, the violence and evil has a purpose, and while it may not be fully historically accurate, the point is made and the emotions are evoked in the viewer. In the Northman, the violence and evil doesn't stop, and it seems to serve only to shock and disgust the viewer. It's dark and horrible just for the sake of being dark and horrible, and while that might work for somebody out there, I'm just not that person. I loved Gladiator because I could feel for Maximus and his struggle to avenge his family. Amleth is just angry and likes killing people. This movie probably isn't trying to be Gladiator or The Patriot, but for me those movies resonate in a way that this one misses the mark on.

Unfortunately, I feel like this is Eggers weakest work. The cinematography was always entertaining but the movie did everything in its power to kill the vibe. In the beginning, everyone has an incredible look but throughout the story, they just downgrade the looks from long haired vikings to some village peasants. The setting in the begging was perfect, but then they go out into the middle of Iceland with nothing to interact with.

I think the biggest consideration of period pieces is that their programming of speech and behaviour is of a time where different things were at stake, largely because ritual and power were at the forefront of the status quo, rather than, for an easy example, the possibility of the static lifestyle one can live now, of which human expedition then would ensure seriousness and expectation be within every walk of isolated thought and shared interaction. It’s against this backdrop that the opening stages’ questionable editing choices become most apparent: establishing that kind of world demands relaxation of a viewer’s experience through integration methods that are timeless in human history, and the film stumbles slightly out of the gate in giving us our footing. It is then the filmmaker’s job to ensure a universal entry point for even the most unintelligent of audience members to understand what is going on. Whilst it doesn’t contain the outstanding personality of The Lighthouse, instead here chasing spectacle in the traditional, predictable form (against its own intended “wow” factor) of “thing happens, get ready for next thing happening!! NEXT THING ARRIVES,” it does unquestionably provide the same fly-on-the-wall approach to that earlier work, giving us full spectator view of a meticulously designed production whose scale no one could argue with, and it’s here that the texture, where production design meets framing, makes a big bang. Where I’m less convinced is the camerawork itself. Eggers leans mechanical: constant pans, deliberate moves, in a way that keeps reminding you it’s camerawork rather than photography. These are undeniably seamless and the level of choreography required is evident in the final product, which is arguably perfect in achieving its intended circuitry (THE SEIGE!), yet there are moments that would’ve landed harder as a single, cleverly framed image of directed blocking, as a still image instead of motion for revelatory sake.
